teile.einleitung: The fennec fox is a small desert fox from North Africa with huge ears. It is the smallest species of the dog family and is perfectly adapted to heat and dryness. During the day it sleeps in cool burrows under the sand, and at night it goes hunting.
wichtigste: The fennec fox belongs to the dog family (Canidae) and to the genus Vulpes.
It is the smallest species of the dog family.
A fully grown fennec fox weighs only about 1 to 2 kilograms.
In relation to body size, its ears are the largest of any member of the dog family.
It lives in the Sahara and other deserts of North Africa.
The name “fennec” comes from Arabic.
According to DNA studies, its closest living relative is the Afghan fox.

abschnitte.text: The fennec fox is a tiny fox: head and body measure about 30 to 40 centimetres, and the bushy tail about 20 to 30 centimetres. Its fur is cream to sandy yellow and camouflages it in the desert sand. Especially striking are the huge **ears**, which grow to about 10 centimetres long in males. The soles of its feet are also thickly furred, so that it does not burn itself on the hot sand.

The fennec fox lives in the sandy deserts of North Africa, mainly in the **Sahara**, and on the Sinai Peninsula. The large ears give off heat and so help to cool the body. During the day it stays in its underground **burrow**, where it is much cooler than on the surface. It can manage for a very long time without drinking and gets a lot of water from its food.

Fennec foxes are **nocturnal** and hunt mainly in the dark. With their large ears they can even hear insects and mice moving under the sand. They eat insects, small rodents, lizards, birds' eggs, and roots and fruit. In a flash they dig their prey out of the sand.

Fennec foxes live in small family groups and dig widely branching burrows together. In spring the female usually gives birth to two to five young. Both parents look after the young, and the male brings food to the family. Fennec foxes communicate with barks, growls and whimpers.

The name “fennec” comes from **Arabic** and means fox. The German naturalist Eberhard August Wilhelm von Zimmermann first described it scientifically in 1780 under the name Canis zerda. Today it is classified as Vulpes zerda in the **genus** of true foxes. The fennec fox is the national animal of Algeria and is not considered threatened overall.

begriffe.erklaerung: A family of predators that includes dogs, wolves and foxes.
An animal that is out and about at night and sleeps during the day.
A hole the animal digs itself in the ground, in which animals live.
A group of closely related species in biology.

gewusst: Algeria's national football team has the nickname “Les Fennecs”.
With its powerful hind legs, the fennec fox can jump surprisingly high and far.
A fennec fox is smaller than many house cats.

teile.einleitung: Mantises are predatory insects with powerful grasping legs, with which they seize prey in a flash. The best-known species is the praying mantis, which also occurs in Switzerland. It has its name because it holds its front legs as if it were praying.
wichtigste: Mantises are insects that belong to the predators.
There are around 2,400 species worldwide, most of them in warm countries.
They hold their prey fast with the spines on their grasping legs.
Their closest relatives are cockroaches and termites.
Praying mantises can turn their triangular head a long way round.
They lay their eggs in an egg case, the ootheca.
In Switzerland, the European praying mantis lives mainly in warm places.

abschnitte.text: Mantises have a long, narrow body and an elongated front section of the thorax. Seen from the front, their head is triangular and has two large **compound eyes**. The praying mantis can turn its head a long way and so look over its shoulder. The front legs have been converted into **grasping legs** set with sharp spines. The European praying mantis is usually green or brown and grows to about 7.5 centimetres long.

Mantises are **ambush hunters** that sit quietly on flowers or twigs. They find their prey mainly with their eyes. When an insect comes close enough, the grasping legs shoot forward in a split second, and the spines hold the prey fast. Most praying mantises have only a single ear in the middle of the body, with which they can hear bats, for example.

The female lays her eggs in a foam that later hardens. This egg case is called an **ootheca** and protects the eggs in winter. In early summer many small larvae hatch, which look like tiny adults. Newly hatched praying mantises eat very small insects such as aphids or fruit flies. Before they are adult, they moult several times, often five to ten times.

Most of the roughly 2,400 species live in the tropics and subtropics. Some look like flowers, like the **orchid mantis** from South-East Asia, others like dry twigs or leaves. In this way they are well camouflaged, both from enemies and from their prey. In terms of relationship, they are closest to cockroaches and termites.

In Switzerland, the **European praying mantis** lives mainly in warm, dry areas. These include the Valais, Ticino and warm slopes at the southern foot of the Jura. As it is getting warmer, it can now also be found in new places on the Central Plateau. It is completely harmless to people and should be left in peace.

begriffe.erklaerung: Front legs that snap shut like a folding knife and seize prey.
A hardened foam case in which the eggs lie protected.
Shedding the old skin that has become too small as the animal grows.
An eye made of many tiny single eyes, typical of insects.

gewusst: Sometimes the female praying mantis eats the male during mating, but far from always.
Praying mantises can turn their heads, and so seem to be looking at you.
With their single ear, many mantises hear the ultrasound of bats and dodge them in flight.

teile.einleitung: Fishing means catching fish and other water animals in order to eat or sell them. It is one of the oldest activities of humankind. In Switzerland, professional fishers fish on the lakes, and many people go angling in their free time.
wichtigste: Fishing is the catching of fish and other water animals.
A distinction is made between professional fishing, which earns money, and recreational fishing with a rod.
Professional fishers on Swiss lakes mostly catch perch and whitefish with nets.
Worldwide, many fish are caught at sea with large ships.
Too much fishing is called overfishing, and it endangers many fish stocks.
Closed seasons and minimum sizes make sure that enough fish grow up.
Anyone who wants to go angling in Switzerland usually needs a licence and proof of competence.

abschnitte.text: In **fishing**, people catch fish, crustaceans, mussels or other water animals. Even in the Stone Age, people used spears, hooks made of bone and traps made of willow twigs. The lake dwellers on Swiss lakes also fished several thousand years ago. Today a distinction is made between **professional fishing** and **recreational fishing**, that is, angling as a hobby.

On lakes such as Lake Constance, Lake Geneva or Lake Neuchâtel, professional fishers still work. They usually go out early in the morning in small boats. They often catch perch with **gill nets**, which stand in the water overnight. The most important fish for them are whitefish and perch. The number of professional fishers has fallen sharply in recent decades, because catches have become smaller.

Most of the fish in the world come from the sea. Large fishing vessels pull huge **trawl nets** through the water or lay out lines many kilometres long with hooks. Herring, cod, tuna and sardines, for example, are caught. Some ships are floating factories on which the fish are processed and frozen straight away. In the process, other animals such as dolphins or turtles often end up in the net as **bycatch**.

Many people in Switzerland go angling on rivers, streams and lakes. For this they usually need a **fishing licence** from the canton. Anyone who is new has to do a course with a **proof of competence**. There you learn to identify fish and to kill them quickly and humanely. There are also rules on which fish you may take, when, and from what size.

If more fish are caught than can grow back, it is called **overfishing**. Worldwide, many sea fish stocks are considered overfished or fully exploited. That is why there are **closed seasons**, during which the fish may spawn undisturbed. A **minimum size** sets how big a fish must be before you may keep it. Quality labels on packaging help shoppers to recognise fish from sustainable fishing.

begriffe.erklaerung: Someone who earns a living by catching fish.
A net that stands like a wall in the water and in which fish get caught.
Animals that end up in the net unintentionally.
When more fish are caught than can grow back.
A time of year when a species of fish may not be caught.

gewusst: A large share of the perch served as perch fillets in Swiss restaurants does not come from Swiss lakes but is imported.
Fishers on Lake Constance often call the perch “Kretzer”.
Even the lake dwellers on Swiss lakes used nets and fish hooks made of bone.

teile.einleitung: Sloths are mammals from the rainforests of Central and South America that hang upside down in the trees for almost their whole lives. They move so slowly that algae even grow on their fur. Their slowness is not a defect, however, but a clever way of saving energy.
wichtigste: Sloths belong to the superorder Xenarthra.
Their closest living relatives are the anteaters.
Depending on the classification, there are six or seven living species.
A distinction is made between two-toed and three-toed sloths, counting the claws on the front legs.
The claws can grow to around 8 to 10 centimetres long.
Three-toed sloths usually have 8 to 9 neck vertebrae and can turn their head about 270 degrees.
Sloths spend most of their time hanging from branches with their backs downward.

abschnitte.text: Sloths have a round head, small ears and dense, shaggy fur. Depending on the species they weigh about 4 to 8 kilograms. On their front legs they have two or three long, curved **claws**, with which they hold on to branches like hooks. Green **algae** often grow in their hair, which camouflage them well in the foliage. Because they usually hang upside down, their fur grows from the belly towards the back, so that rainwater runs off well.

The **three-toed sloths** belong to the genus Bradypus, which in Greek means “slow foot”. The **two-toed sloths** are called Choloepus, that is, “lame foot”. Three-toed sloths usually have 8 to 9 neck vertebrae instead of the usual 7. Two-toed sloths, by contrast, have only 5 to 7 neck vertebrae, depending on the animal. Both groups belong to the **Xenarthra**, named after extra joints in the chest and lower back vertebrae.

Sloths live in the tropical rainforests of Central and South America. They eat mainly leaves, which provide little energy and are hard to digest. Their stomach has several chambers, and digesting a meal often takes several days to weeks. Sloths therefore have a very slow **metabolism** and a rather low body temperature.

Sloths sleep and rest for many hours a day, usually well hidden in the treetops. Only about once a week do they climb down to the ground to relieve themselves. On the ground they are very clumsy, but in the water they are surprisingly good **swimmers**. Their slowness also protects them, because predators such as the harpy eagle or the jaguar find it harder to spot them.

About 10,000 years ago, **giant sloths** such as Megatherium, which could grow as large as an elephant, still lived in the Americas. They walked on the ground and died out at the end of the last Ice Age. Today the pygmy three-toed sloth, on a small island off Panama, is especially seriously threatened. The clearing of rainforests also endangers many sloths.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of mammals with extra joints in the spine, including sloths, anteaters and armadillos.
All the processes in the body by which food is turned into energy.
The bones of the spine in the neck.
Simple green living things that grow in water or in damp places.

gewusst: In sloths' fur live whole communities of algae, beetles and small moths.
When diving, sloths can slow their breathing a great deal and stay under water for a long time.
Even after death, sloths sometimes stay hanging from branches by their claws.

teile.einleitung: Eutrophication means that a body of water contains too many nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen. Algae then grow very strongly, and oxygen can become scarce in the deep water. Many Swiss lakes suffered from this in the 1960s and 1970s, and fish such as whitefish had problems.
wichtigste: Eutrophication is the over-fertilising of a body of water with nutrients.
The most important nutrients involved are phosphorus and nitrogen.
With too many nutrients, algae grow very strongly.
When dead algae are broken down, oxygen is used up.
A lack of oxygen can develop in the deep water.
In the 1960s and 1970s, whitefish therefore did worse in many lakes.
Sewage treatment plants and the ban on phosphates in washing powders have made Swiss lakes cleaner again.

abschnitte.text: The word **eutrophication** comes from Greek and means roughly “well fed”. It means that a lake, river or sea receives too many **nutrients**. **Phosphorus** and nitrogen in particular act like fertiliser in water. A little of them is needed, but too much upsets the balance.

First, algae and water plants grow much more strongly than normal, and sometimes the water turns green. This is called an **algal bloom**. When the algae die, they sink to the bottom, where bacteria break them down. In doing so, the bacteria use up so much oxygen that a lack of oxygen develops in the deep water.

abschnitte.titel: Where do the nutrients come from?
abschnitte.text: Many nutrients come from **agriculture**, for example from slurry and fertiliser washed from fields into the water. In the past a lot of phosphate also came from household waste water, especially from washing powders. Waste water from industry and from settlements without good treatment also contributed. In lakes the nutrients build up over many years.

If the deep water lacks oxygen, no fish and hardly any small animals can live there any more. **Whitefish**, whose eggs develop on the lake bed, were especially affected. In the 1960s and 1970s they therefore did worse in many Swiss lakes. With a severe lack of oxygen, fish can even die in large numbers.

From the 1960s, Switzerland built **sewage treatment plants** in almost every municipality, which remove phosphorus from waste water. Since 1986, phosphate in laundry detergents has been banned in Switzerland. In some heavily polluted lakes such as Lake Baldegg, Lake Sempach and Lake Hallwil, oxygen is also fed into the deep water. Today many lakes are clear again, but smaller lakes on the Central Plateau are still partly polluted because of agriculture.

Lakes can also become richer in nutrients naturally over thousands of years and slowly silt up. Eutrophication caused by people, however, happens much faster. Experts therefore regularly measure phosphorus, oxygen and algae in the lakes. In this way they can tell early on whether a body of water is in danger again.

begriffe.erklaerung: Substances that plants and algae need in order to grow.
A strong increase of algae that colours the water.
A plant that cleans dirty waste water.
A substance containing phosphorus that acts like fertiliser.

gewusst: Lake Baldegg in the canton of Lucerne has been artificially aerated with compressed air and oxygen since the 1980s.
Seas can also be over-fertilised, for example the Baltic Sea, where large areas short of oxygen have formed on the sea floor.

teile.einleitung: River dolphins are dolphins that live not in the sea but in large rivers, for example the Amazon or the Ganges. They have long, narrow beaks and often only tiny eyes. All river dolphins are rare today and seriously threatened.
wichtigste: River dolphins live in large rivers of South America and Asia.
The best known is the pink Amazon river dolphin.
They have long, narrow beaks with many teeth.
In murky river water they find their way mainly by echolocation.
The river dolphins of India and Pakistan are almost blind.
The Chinese river dolphin has been considered probably extinct since 2006.
Dams, fishing nets and water pollution threaten all species.

abschnitte.text: **River dolphins** are toothed whales that have adapted to life in fresh water. They are not a single closely related group, but several old lines that moved into rivers independently of one another. Typical are a long, narrow **beak** with many pointed teeth and a flexible neck. Their dorsal fin is often only a low hump. Most have small eyes, because you can see little in muddy water anyway.

The **Amazon river dolphin**, called the boto in Brazil, lives in the Amazon and the Orinoco in South America. It is the largest river dolphin and can grow to about 2.5 metres long. Adult animals, especially the males, are often strikingly **pink**. In the rainy season, when the forests are flooded, it swims between tree trunks. For this it can turn its head a long way and is very agile.

In the Ganges and Brahmaputra in India and Bangladesh lives the **Ganges river dolphin**, and in the Indus in Pakistan the Indus river dolphin. Their eyes have no lens, and they can probably only tell light from dark. They therefore rely entirely on their **echolocation**. The **Chinese river dolphin**, or baiji, from the Yangtze was no longer found in a large search in 2006. Since then it has been considered probably extinct.

River dolphins give out clicking sounds and hear the echo, like bats. In this way they find fish, crustaceans and turtles in muddy water and on the bottom. With their long beak they root out prey between roots and in the mud. They mostly live alone or in small groups. Females have a young one only every few years.

All river dolphins are considered **endangered** or critically endangered today. Dams cut up their habitats and separate the populations from one another. Many animals drown as bycatch in fishing nets. Added to that are waste water, mercury from gold mines and heavy boat traffic. In several countries there are protected areas and programmes that count the populations and involve the fishers.

begriffe.erklaerung: A whale with teeth, for example a dolphin or sperm whale.
Finding the way using sounds and their echo.
Water in rivers and lakes that contains hardly any salt.
Animals that end up unintentionally in fishing nets.

gewusst: On the Amazon, an old legend says the boto turns into an elegant man at night.
The Ganges river dolphin sometimes swims on its side and feels the bottom with a flipper.
The Chinese river dolphin was probably the first species of whale to be wiped out by humans.

teile.einleitung: The rockhopper penguin is a small, cheeky penguin with yellow tufts of feathers above its eyes that look like wild hair. It lives on rocky islands in the south of the world. It has its name because it hops skilfully over rocks.
wichtigste: The rockhopper penguin has yellow, bristly feathers above its eyes.
It belongs to the crested penguins.
At about 50 centimetres it is one of the smaller penguins.
It lives on islands in the southern Atlantic and Indian Oceans, for example on the Falkland Islands.
Instead of waddling, it often hops over rocks with both feet together.
The rockhopper penguin is considered vulnerable.

abschnitte.text: The rockhopper penguin grows to about 50 to 55 centimetres tall and usually weighs 2 to 3 kilograms. Its back and head are black, and its belly is white. Above its red eyes it has a yellow **crest** of long, bristly feathers that stick out sideways. Its short, strong beak is orange-red.

Rockhopper penguins live on islands in cool seas south of South America, Africa and Australia. Important colonies are on the **Falkland Islands** and on islands in the southern Indian Ocean. Today a distinction is usually made between the southern and the northern rockhopper penguin. They breed on steep, rocky coasts where the surf is strong.

Rockhopper penguins eat mainly **krill**, small crustaceans, squid and small fish. They hunt in the sea and often dive several dozen metres deep. With their wings, which have become **flippers**, they “fly” under water. On land they cannot fly, but they are very skilful climbers.

Rockhopper penguins breed in large, noisy **colonies**. The female lays two eggs, the first of which is clearly smaller. Usually only the chick from the larger second egg survives. When climbing, they hop from stone to stone with both feet at the same time, which is why they are called “rockhoppers” in English.

The number of rockhopper penguins has fallen sharply in recent decades. The reasons are warmer sea water, less food, fishing and pollution by **oil**. The species is therefore listed as vulnerable on the Red List. Protected areas and less fishing in their hunting grounds are meant to help them.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of penguins with yellow tufts of feathers on the head.
Small, shrimp-like crustaceans that live in large swarms in the sea.
A large group of animals that breed together in the same place.
A list of the animal and plant species that are threatened with extinction.

gewusst: Rockhopper penguins jump up surprisingly high rock steps with both feet at once.
Their English name “rockhopper” means roughly “rock hopper”.
The first egg of the rockhopper penguin is clearly smaller than the second.

teile.einleitung: The hippopotamus (in German “Flusspferd”, literally “river horse”) is one of the largest land animals on Earth and spends the day almost always in the water. It looks comfortable but is regarded as one of the most dangerous animals in Africa. Its second German name is “Nilpferd”, meaning “Nile horse”.
wichtigste: Hippopotamuses live mainly in Africa south of the Sahara.
During the day they lie in the water to cool off and to shelter from the sun.
Eyes, ears and nose are on top of the head so that the animal can almost completely submerge.
Hippopotamuses are plant-eaters and eat mainly grass.
A fully grown female weighs about 1,500 kilograms.
A female is called a cow, the young one a calf, and a group a herd.
In Switzerland you can see hippopotamuses at Basel Zoo, for example.

abschnitte.text: The hippopotamus has a massive, barrel-shaped body and short, powerful legs. A fully grown animal weighs about 1,500 kilograms, and large bulls can weigh clearly more. The **skin** is several centimetres thick and almost hairless. In the huge mouth are long canine teeth called **tusks**, which can be over 50 centimetres long.

Hippopotamuses live in rivers, lakes and swamps in Africa south of the Sahara. By day they doze in the water, because their sensitive skin dries out quickly in the sun. Because their eyes, ears and nostrils are on top of the head, they can breathe, see and hear almost completely submerged. Under water they close their ears and **nostrils** and can hold their breath for several minutes. They can hardly really swim, and mostly walk along the bottom.

Although hippopotamuses are dangerous, they are **plant-eaters**. At night they leave the water and go to graze on land. Their main food is **grass**, which they pull off with their broad lips. In one night they eat many kilograms of grass and often cover several kilometres as they do so.

Hippopotamuses live in a **herd**, which is usually led by a strong bull. A female is called a cow and carries her young one in her belly for about eight months. The **calf** is often born in the water and can also feed there. The mother always stays very close to it and defends it bravely against crocodiles, lions or strange bulls.

Hippopotamuses defend their territory fiercely and can run faster than a person on land. That is why dangerous encounters with people keep happening in Africa. At the same time the hippopotamus is itself threatened, because its habitat is shrinking and it is hunted for its meat and for the **ivory** of its teeth. On the Red List it is considered vulnerable. In Switzerland you can watch hippopotamuses at **Basel Zoo**, for example.

begriffe.erklaerung: Very long, powerful canine teeth, for example in the hippopotamus or wild boar.
A group of animals that lives together.
An animal that feeds on plants such as grass or leaves.
A list that shows how seriously animal and plant species are threatened.

gewusst: The closest living relatives of the hippopotamus are the whales.
Hippopotamuses give off a reddish liquid that protects their skin like a sun cream.
Bulls mark their territory with their dung by flinging it about wildly with their tails.

teile.einleitung: Rorquals are a family of large whales that includes the blue whale, the largest animal that has ever lived. They have their name from the many grooves on the throat and belly. These grooves allow them to take huge amounts of water with food into the mouth.
wichtigste: Rorquals belong to the baleen whales.
The blue whale also belongs to the baleen whales and is a rorqual.
The rorquals include the blue whale, fin whale, humpback whale, sei whale and minke whale.
On the throat and belly they have long grooves that can expand like a balloon.
Instead of teeth they have baleen, with which they sieve food from the water.
They eat mainly krill and small shoaling fish.
Many rorquals were hunted heavily in the past and are still rare today.

abschnitte.text: The rorquals are a family within the **baleen whales**. Typical of them are a slim, streamlined body and a small dorsal fin. On the underside of the throat and chest run numerous long **throat grooves**. They include the blue whale, the fin whale, the sei whale, Bryde's whale, the minke whale and the humpback whale.

Rorquals have no teeth but **baleen**, which are horn plates hanging down from the upper jaw. When feeding, the whale takes in a huge gulp of water with krill or fish, and the throat grooves expand greatly. Then it pushes the water out again through the baleen with its tongue. The food stays caught as in a sieve and is swallowed.

The **blue whale** is the largest animal that has ever lived on Earth, larger than any dinosaur. It can grow to around 30 metres long and weigh well over 100 tonnes. The fin whale is the second largest whale and a particularly fast swimmer. The smallest rorqual is the minke whale, at about 8 to 10 metres long.

Many rorquals migrate long distances every year between cold feeding grounds and warmer seas, where they have their young. The **humpback whale** is known for its long songs and for spectacular leaps out of the water. Rorquals communicate with deep sounds that can be heard very far away in the water. Like all whales, they are **mammals**, breathe air and suckle their young.

In the 19th and 20th centuries, rorquals were hunted in great numbers for their blubber and meat. This brought the blue whale almost to extinction. Since 1986 there has been a worldwide ban on commercial **whaling**, although not all countries keep to it. Today the whales are also threatened by collisions with ships, noise in the sea, fishing nets and climate change.

begriffe.erklaerung: Horn plates in the mouth of baleen whales that work like a sieve.
Small, shrimp-like crustaceans that live in huge swarms in the sea.
Long folds on the underside of the whale that stretch when it feeds.
An animal whose young are suckled with milk.

gewusst: A blue whale can eat several tonnes of krill in a day.
The heart of a blue whale is about as big as a small car.

teile.einleitung: The pheasant family is a large family of gamebirds. It includes well-known animals such as the domestic chicken, the peacock and the common pheasant. Many of them live on the ground and are true masters at scratching and running.
wichtigste: The pheasant family belongs to the order of gamebirds.
The family includes the pheasant, the domestic chicken and the peacock.
So the cockerel and the peacock belong to the same family.
Most species look for their food on the ground.
In many species the males are much more colourful than the females.
In Switzerland, for example, the capercaillie, the black grouse and the rock ptarmigan live.

abschnitte.text: Members of the pheasant family have a strong body, short, round wings and powerful legs for scratching. In many species the **cocks** are splendidly coloured, while the hens are camouflaged in plain brown. The best-known example is the **peacock** with its long, shimmering display feathers. The common pheasant also has a long tail and a red patch on its head.

The family includes well over a hundred species. Many come originally from Asia, for example the peacock from India and Sri Lanka. The domestic chicken descends from the **red junglefowl**, which lives in the forests of South-East Asia. The common pheasant actually comes from Asia and was released in Europe for hunting. According to the current classification, the grey partridge, the quail and the grouse also belong to it.

Members of the pheasant family eat mainly seeds, grains, buds, berries and leaves. With their feet they scratch in the soil and so also find worms and insects. Chicks need especially many insects, because they need a lot of protein to grow. Small stones in the stomach help to grind up hard grains.

In spring the males court the females with a striking **display**: they call, dance or spread a fan of feathers. Most species build their nest well hidden on the ground. The chicks are **precocial**: they can run and peck soon after hatching. To keep their feathers clean, many members of the pheasant family take a sand bath.

The domestic chicken is one of the most important farm animals in the world and provides eggs and meat. In Switzerland, wild relatives live there, such as the **capercaillie**, the black grouse, the hazel grouse and the rock ptarmigan. The capercaillie has become rare and needs quiet, open mountain forests. The grey partridge has almost completely disappeared in Switzerland, because it lacks hedges and fallow land.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of birds with strong legs that includes chickens, pheasants and quails.
The males' courting of a female with dances, calls and decorative feathers.
Young animals that can leave the nest right after hatching.
Gamebirds with feathered legs, for example the capercaillie.

gewusst: All the domestic chickens in the world descend from the wild red junglefowl of South-East Asia.
The Indian peafowl is the national bird of India.
The rock ptarmigan has white plumage in winter and greyish brown plumage in summer.

teile.einleitung: Lichens look like plants, but they are a partnership between a fungus and an alga or a cyanobacterium. They grow on stones, tree bark and walls and survive even in the coldest and driest places on Earth. Because they react sensitively to air pollution, they tell us how clean the air is.
wichtigste: Lichens are partnerships between a fungus and an alga or cyanobacterium.
The fungus offers protection and water, the alga makes food by photosynthesis.
A distinction is made between crustose, foliose and fruticose lichens.
Lichens grow very slowly, often only a few millimetres a year.
They can survive extreme cold, heat and dryness.
Many lichens show whether the air is clean.
Reindeer lichen is an important food for reindeer in the far north.

abschnitte.text: A **lichen** consists of two very different living things that work together. A fungus forms the framework and protects, and tiny algae or **cyanobacteria** live inside it. These make sugar from sunlight by **photosynthesis**, which the fungus also lives on. In return the fungus supplies water, minerals and protection from drying out. Such a partnership for mutual benefit is called **symbiosis**.

Crustose lichens lie like a coloured layer of paint firmly on stones or bark. Foliose lichens are flat and lobed and can be lifted off a little. **Fruticose lichens** grow like small bushes or hang from branches as beards, such as the beard lichens in mountain forests. Lichens come in yellow, orange, grey, green and even black. Many thousands of species are known worldwide.

Lichens grow in places where hardly anything else can live: on bare rock, in the mountains, in deserts and even in Antarctica. When it is dry, they fall into a kind of stiffness and wake up again as soon as they get wet. In return, they grow extremely slowly, often only a few millimetres a year. Some lichens can be hundreds or even thousands of years old. In the Swiss Alps, rocks often glow yellow-green with the **map lichen**.

The **reindeer lichen** grows in the cold regions of the north as grey, branched cushions. In winter, reindeer dig it out from under the snow, and it is their most important food there. In the past, lichens were used to dye wool. The dye litmus, with which acids are recognised in chemistry lessons, also comes from a lichen. In nature, lichens help to weather rock slowly and to form soil.

Lichens take up water and substances directly from the air and rain. That is why many species react sensitively to pollutants such as sulphur dioxide. Where the air is heavily polluted, the sensitive species disappear. Experts therefore use lichens as **bioindicators**. Since the air in Switzerland has become cleaner, more lichens are returning in many towns.

begriffe.erklaerung: Different living things living together for mutual benefit.
Making sugar from light, water and carbon dioxide.
Tiny bacteria that carry out photosynthesis like plants.
A living thing that shows how healthy the environment is.

gewusst: Lichens survived unprotected in space for several days when researchers sent them into space in an experiment.
Because the map lichen grows so evenly slowly, it can be used to estimate how long a rock has been free of glacier ice.
The litmus paper from chemistry lessons owes its dye to a lichen.

teile.einleitung: The European catfish is the largest pure freshwater fish in Europe. It can grow to over two metres long and has a wide mouth with long barbels. A nocturnal predator, it lives hidden on the bottom of lakes and large rivers.
wichtigste: The catfish is a fish, and its scientific name is Silurus glanis.
It can grow to over two metres long.
It has six barbels around its mouth.
Its skin has no scales and is slimy.
It is mainly active at dusk and at night.
It eats fish, frogs, crayfish and sometimes waterbirds.
The catfish keeps growing all its life.

abschnitte.text: The catfish has a long body, a wide, flat head and a huge mouth. Around its mouth it has six **barbels**, two long ones on the upper jaw and four short ones on the lower jaw. Its skin has no scales and is slimy, dark on top and pale on the belly. Inside the mouth are many small, fine teeth like a rasp, which it uses to hold on to its prey.

The European catfish is the largest pure freshwater fish in Europe. It keeps growing all its life and can reach over two metres in length. Large animals weigh well over 100 kilograms. Such giants are rare, though, and most catfish are much smaller.

The catfish lives in warm, slow-flowing rivers and in lakes with a soft bottom. Originally it is found mainly in eastern and central Europe, for example around the River Danube. In Switzerland it lives in places such as **Lake Murten**, **Lake Biel** and the Rhine. When the water is high, it likes to stay in flooded areas along the banks.

Catfish are mainly active at dusk and at night. They move slowly and smoothly close to the bottom of the water. With their barbels they feel and taste their surroundings, and a delicate **lateral line organ** senses movements in the water. A fully grown catfish eats fish, frogs, crayfish and sometimes waterbirds.

Catfish spawn in early summer, when the water is warm. The male builds a kind of **nest** out of plants in shallow water. There the female lays tens of thousands of eggs. The male guards the nest until the young fish have hatched.

As predators, catfish keep other fish populations in check and often eat sick or weak animals. Because the water is getting warmer, they are spreading in many waters. Some anglers worry that catfish eat too many other fish. The catfish is harmless to people, and its meat is considered tasty.

begriffe.erklaerung: Threads around a fish's mouth that it uses to feel and taste.
A fish that hunts and eats other animals.
Without scales on the skin.
A sense organ on the side of fish that detects movements in the water.

gewusst: In southern France, researchers have watched catfish leap briefly out of the water onto the bank to catch pigeons.
A large catfish can be as long as a grown person is tall.

teile.einleitung: The udder is the part of the body from which milk comes in cows, goats and sheep. It hangs between the back legs and is made up of mammary glands and teats. Without the udder there would be no milk for the calves, and no cheese, yoghurt or butter.
wichtigste: The udder is the mammary gland of cows, goats, sheep and other hoofed animals.
The cow's milk comes from the udder.
A cow's udder normally has four teats.
A goat's udder usually has two teats.
An udder only gives milk after the animal has given birth to a young one.
In Switzerland, most cows are milked with a milking machine.
A healthy udder is very important for the quality of the milk.

abschnitte.text: The **udder** is a large mammary gland that lies between the back legs of cows, goats, sheep and horses. It is one of the mammary glands that all mammals have. With it, mothers feed their young in the first weeks and months. In cows the udder is especially large, because they have been bred for a long time to give a lot of milk.

A cow's udder is made up of four separate **quarters**, and each quarter has its own **teat**. Goats and sheep have an udder with two halves and usually two teats. Inside, tiny sacs make the milk from the blood. For this, a great deal of blood has to flow through the udder, several hundred litres for one litre of milk.

A cow only gives milk after she has had a calf. The first milk is called **colostrum** and is especially important for the calf's defences against disease. After that the cow gives milk for many months, as long as she is milked regularly. Before the next birth the udder gets a rest, which is called the **dry period**.

In the past cows were milked by hand, but today it is mostly done with a milking machine or a milking robot. In Switzerland there are around half a million dairy cows (as of 2024). A cow is usually milked twice a day. Products such as cheese, butter and yoghurt are made from the milk, for example the well-known Emmental or Gruyère.

A common illness is **mastitis**, in which bacteria get into the udder. The milk is then changed and may not be sold. Farmers therefore take care to keep the barns clean and clean the teats before milking. Enough space and fresh straw also help to keep the udder healthy.

begriffe.erklaerung: The part of the udder from which the milk comes out.
An organ that makes milk.
The very first milk after birth, full of substances that fight disease.
A machine that milks cows by itself when they come to it.

gewusst: Today a cow often gives over 20 litres of milk a day.
Cows often go to the milking robot of their own accord, because they get food there.

teile.einleitung: A fish farm is an operation in which fish are deliberately kept, bred and raised. Some of the fish later end up on the plate, while others are released as young fish into lakes and rivers. Worldwide today, about half of the fish eaten come from farms.
wichtigste: In a fish farm, fish are deliberately bred and raised.
Fish farming in ponds or tanks is also called aquaculture.
In Switzerland, mainly trout are farmed.
Hatcheries hatch the eggs of whitefish and lake trout and release young fish.
This release of young fish is called stocking.
Fish farming can take pressure off the seas, but also brings problems.
Even in the Middle Ages, monks farmed carp in monastery ponds.

abschnitte.text: A **fish farm** is a place where trout, carp, salmon or other fish are deliberately bred and raised. The fish live in ponds, concrete tanks, net cages in the sea or in halls with circulating water. Experts call the farming of water animals **aquaculture**. The fish are fed, and their water quality is constantly monitored. After a few months to years, they have reached the right size to sell.

First, eggs and milt are obtained from adult fish ready to spawn by gently stripping them. The fertilised eggs then lie in hatching jars or hatching troughs with fresh, cool water. After a few weeks, small larvae hatch with a **yolk sac**, from which they first feed. After that they are given fine food and carry on growing in larger tanks. Clean water, enough oxygen and little stress are important.

Many cantons run **fish hatcheries**. In winter, fishers catch whitefish ready to spawn and collect their eggs. These are hatched in the hatchery, and the young fish are then released back into the lakes. For the **lake trout**, animals ready to spawn are caught in the feeder streams and their eggs are hatched in facilities. This release of young fish is called **stocking**.

In Switzerland, mainly **rainbow trout** are raised in food fish farms, along with char, perch and a few other species. Even so, most of the fish that people in Switzerland eat is imported. Salmon in the shop mostly comes from large net pens in the sea, for example in Norway. Worldwide, most farmed fish are produced in Asia, above all in China. Carp are among the most widely farmed fish in the world.

Fish farming can help to protect the seas from **overfishing**. But in large farms, many animals live in a small space, and diseases or parasites spread easily. Sometimes farmed fish escape and mix with wild members of their species. Predatory fish such as salmon are partly fed with fishmeal made from wild catches. Quality labels show whether a farm cares about animal welfare and the environment.

begriffe.erklaerung: Farming of fish and other water animals under human control.
A facility in which fish eggs are hatched.
Releasing young fish into lakes or rivers.
A store of nutrients on the belly of newly hatched fish larvae.

gewusst: The rainbow trout originally comes from North America and was brought to Europe for farming.
In the Middle Ages, monks farmed carp because during Lent they were allowed to eat fish instead of meat.
In a single hatching jar, tens of thousands of whitefish eggs can develop at the same time.

teile.einleitung: Frugivores are animals that live mainly on fruit. In German they are called “Fruchtfresser”, which means fruit-eaters. They play an important role in nature because they spread the seeds of plants.
wichtigste: Animals that live mainly on fruit are called fruit-eaters, or frugivores.
The word comes from Latin: fructus means fruit and vorare means to devour.
Many frugivores live in tropical rainforests, where fruit grows all year round.
Examples are flying foxes, toucans, orang-utans and many parrots.
Frugivores spread plant seeds in their droppings.
In Switzerland, too, birds such as blackbirds and thrushes like to eat berries.
Many frugivores also eat leaves, insects or nectar as well.

abschnitte.text: A **frugivore** is an animal whose food consists for the most part of fruit. Fruit contains a lot of sugar and water and therefore supplies energy quickly. Few animals eat only fruit, and most supplement their diet with leaves, seeds or insects. Similar terms are **herbivore** for plant-eaters and carnivore for meat-eaters.

Among the best-known frugivores are the **flying foxes**, large chiropterans from Africa, Asia and Australia. Toucans in South America use their huge beak to pick fruit from thin branches. Orang-utans on Borneo and Sumatra like best to eat ripe fruit such as figs. The cassowary, a large flightless bird from New Guinea and Australia, also eats mainly fallen fruit.

When an animal eats a fruit, it often swallows the seeds too. These pass unharmed through the gut and are passed out with the droppings in another place. In this way frugivores help plants to spread. This kind of **seed dispersal** is vital for many rainforest trees, and some seeds even germinate better after passing through a gut.

In Switzerland, too, there are animals that like to eat fruit. Blackbirds, thrushes and the blackcap peck berries of elder, rowan and hawthorn in autumn. In winter, **waxwings** sometimes come from the north and feed almost only on berries. The edible dormouse also likes to eat fruit, nuts and beechnuts.

Many fruits are red, black or orange so that animals can see them easily. The plant attracts the animals with sweet **fruit flesh** and gets help in spreading its seeds in return. This is an example of co-operation for mutual benefit, which is called **symbiosis**. If frugivores disappear, some trees can hardly reproduce any more.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal that feeds mainly on fruit.
A plant-eater.
How seeds get from the parent plant to a new place.
Living together in which both sides gain an advantage.

gewusst: Some flying foxes have a wingspan of over a metre and still eat only fruit and nectar.
Some tree seeds germinate better after passing through an animal's gut.

teile.einleitung: Lacewings are delicate, mostly green insects with large, transparent wings and golden shining eyes. Their larvae are voracious hunters that eat so many aphids that they are called aphid lions. That is why lacewings are very welcome beneficial insects in the garden.
wichtigste: Lacewings are delicate insects with wings veined like a net.
Many species are green and have golden shining eyes.
Their larvae hunt aphids with pincer-like jaws.
Because of their hunger, the larvae are also called aphid lions.
Lacewings lay their eggs on thin stalks.
In organic gardens they are encouraged as beneficial insects, for example with insect hotels.
Some lacewings spend the winter in houses and turn brownish as they do so.

abschnitte.text: **Lacewings** belong to the insect order of the **net-winged insects**. They are about one to two centimetres long and have a slim, usually pale green body. Their four wings are transparent, finely veined and, at rest, folded like a roof over the body. The golden shining eyes are striking, which is why they are also called goldeyes. In Switzerland the **common green lacewing** is especially frequent.

The larvae look quite different from the adults. They are elongated, mobile and have large, **pincer-like jaws** at the front. With these they seize aphids, pierce them and suck them dry. A single larva can eat hundreds of aphids during its development. Because of this voraciousness, they are called **aphid lions**.

The female lays her eggs singly on thin, hair-fine **stalks**, often on leaves near aphid colonies. The stalks protect the eggs from being eaten by ants or by their own siblings. After hatching, the larva eats for about two to three weeks and moults several times. Then it spins a small, round cocoon and pupates. From this the adult lacewing finally emerges.

Adult common green lacewings eat mainly flower pollen, nectar and **honeydew**, the sweet liquid that aphids give off. Other species of lacewing also eat aphids as adults. Lacewings are active mainly at dusk and at night. Some species can detect the ultrasound calls of bats with their wings. Then they drop in a flash so as not to be eaten.

Because the larvae eat so many aphids, lacewings are regarded as important **beneficial insects**. Gardeners and farmers even buy lacewing larvae to use them against pests in greenhouses. This is called **biological pest control**. In an organic garden you help lacewings with flower meadows, insect hotels and special lacewing boxes. In autumn the adults often look for shelter in houses, attics or garden sheds, where they should be left in peace to spend the winter.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of insects with finely veined, net-like wings.
The young form of an insect, which often looks quite different from the adult.
A sweet liquid that aphids give off.
An animal that eats pests and so helps people.

gewusst: Some lacewing larvae camouflage themselves by piling the empty skins of their prey on their backs.
The green common lacewing turns yellowish to brownish in winter and green again in spring.
With an organ in their wings, lacewings can hear the calls of hunting bats.

teile.einleitung: Colour vision is the ability to perceive light of different wavelengths as different colours. People and animals see colours in quite different ways. Some animals see fewer colours than we do, while others even see colours that are invisible to us.
wichtigste: Colours are made in the brain from light of different wavelengths.
The sense cells in the retina called cones are responsible for colour vision.
Humans have three kinds of cone, for red, green and blue.
Dogs see fewer colours than humans, mainly shades of blue and yellow.
Many birds and insects can see ultraviolet light.
About eight per cent of men have red-green colour vision deficiency.

abschnitte.text: Light consists of waves of different **wavelengths**. White sunlight contains all the colours, which you can see in a rainbow. An object looks red because it mainly reflects red light and swallows up the other colours. It is the brain that turns these light signals into the impression of a colour.

In the **retina** at the back of the eye there are two kinds of sense cell. The **rods** are very sensitive to light but do not see colours, which is why everything looks grey at night. The **cones** need more light and are responsible for colour vision. Humans have three kinds of cone, which respond mainly to red, green and blue light. From the mixture of their signals, millions of shades arise.

Dogs and cats have only two kinds of cone and see mainly shades of blue and yellow. They find it hard to tell red and green apart. Many birds have four kinds of cone and can also see **ultraviolet light**. Bees also see UV light, but cannot see red. The mantis shrimp has an especially large number of kinds of light-sensing cell, but still does not necessarily see more colours.

With colours, animals recognise ripe fruit, poisonous animals or a suitable mate. Many flowers have UV patterns that only insects see and that show them the way to the nectar. For people, colours help in everyday life, for example with traffic lights and warning signs. A bull in a bullfight, by the way, does not react to the red colour of the cloth, but to its **movement**.

If one kind of cone is missing or works differently, this is called **colour vision deficiency**. The most common is red-green deficiency, which affects about eight per cent of men but only very few women. The English scientist John Dalton described his own colour blindness in 1794. In the 19th century, Thomas Young and Hermann von Helmholtz explained colour vision with three primary colours.

begriffe.erklaerung: Sense cells in the retina with which we see colours.
Sense cells that tell light from dark in dim light.
The thin layer at the back of the eye that turns light into nerve signals.
Light that is invisible to people but not to many animals.

gewusst: At night, humans see almost no colours, because then only the rods are working.
Some birds see patterns on the feathers of others of their kind that are invisible to us.
After John Dalton, colour blindness is sometimes also called daltonism.

teile.einleitung: Antennae are the two movable feelers on the head of an insect. With them, insects smell, touch and taste their surroundings. They are something like a nose and fingers in one.
wichtigste: Every insect has exactly one pair of antennae on its head.
Another word for antennae is feelers.
With their antennae, insects pick up stimuli from their surroundings, above all smells and touches.
The praying mantis, too, senses smells and touches with its antennae.
In the pond skater, the antennae likewise pick up stimuli from the surroundings.
Antennae can be thread-like, feathery, clubbed or elbowed.
Spiders have no antennae, but crustaceans even have two pairs.

abschnitte.text: **Antennae** are long, movable appendages on the head of insects, centipedes and crustaceans. They consist of many small parts that are called segments. Insects always have exactly one pair of antennae. That is why spiders, which have no antennae, do not belong to the insects.

On the antennae sit thousands of tiny hairs and pores that work as **sense organs**. With them, insects smell scents, taste, touch and sense warmth or moisture. The praying mantis uses its antennae to sense smells and touches. The pond skater uses them to pick up stimuli from its surroundings.

Antennae look quite different depending on the insect. Butterflies that fly by day have thin antennae with a thickening at the end, which is called **clubbed**. Ants have elbowed antennae, and cockchafers have fan-like plates at the tip. The males of some moths carry large, **feathery** antennae that look like small fern leaves.

The males of the silk moth and other moths can smell the scent of a female from a great distance. Such attractants are called **pheromones**. A few scent particles are enough for the male to find his way to the female. Male mosquitoes even hear the buzzing of the females with their bushy antennae.

abschnitte.titel: Antennae in the daily life of insects
abschnitte.text: Ants touch each other with their antennae and in this way recognise whether another animal comes from their own nest. Bees recognise the scent of flowers with their antennae and so find nectar. Because antennae are so important, insects clean them regularly. Ants even have a small notch on their front legs with which they clean their antennae like a **comb**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another word for a feeler.
A part of the body with which a living thing perceives something, for example an eye, an ear or an antenna.
A scent with which animals of the same species send each other messages.
A single link or section, for example of an antenna.

gewusst: The antennae of some longhorn beetles are much longer than their whole body.
Crustaceans such as lobsters have two pairs of antennae, so four instead of two.

teile.einleitung: The feline immunodeficiency virus, FIV for short, is a virus that weakens the defence system of cats. It is related to the human HIV and is therefore sometimes called “cat AIDS”. For people and other pets, however, it is completely harmless.
wichtigste: FIV is the cat immune deficiency virus.
It is similar to the human HIV but cannot be passed on to people.
It is mainly passed on through deep bite wounds in fights.
Especially often affected are unneutered tomcats that go outdoors.
There is no cure, but many cats still live well for years.
A blood test at the vet shows whether a cat has FIV.

abschnitte.text: FIV stands for **feline immunodeficiency virus**, where “feline” means cat-like. It belongs to the **lentiviruses**, a group of viruses that work slowly. It was discovered in 1986 in California in cats with a weakened defence system. The virus attacks certain white blood cells that are important for fighting disease.

The virus is found mainly in the saliva of infected cats. It is usually passed on through deep **bite wounds** in territorial fights. That is why unneutered tomcats that spend a lot of time outside and often fight are especially often affected. When eating together or grooming one another, the virus is only rarely passed on.

After infection, many cats show hardly any signs for years. Over time the **immune system** becomes weaker, and the cat catches other infections more easily. Common examples are inflammation in the mouth, colds or skin problems. Many FIV-positive cats still reach a normal age if they are well looked after.

A **blood test** at the vet shows whether a cat has antibodies against FIV in its blood. The infection cannot be cured. However, the accompanying illnesses can be treated, for example with medicines against bacteria. A healthy diet, little stress and regular check-ups at the vet are especially important.

**Neutering** lowers the risk, because neutered tomcats fight less often. FIV-positive cats live best as indoor cats or with secured balconies, so that they do not infect other cats. They can often live together with peaceful cats that do not bite. There is no **risk of infection** at all for children, adults and dogs.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny germ that causes disease and can multiply only inside living cells.
The body's own defence against disease-causing germs.
Defensive substances in the blood that the body makes against a particular germ.
An operation at the vet after which an animal can no longer have young.

gewusst: FIV does not occur only in house cats; similar viruses exist in lions and pumas too.
Many animal shelters successfully rehome FIV-positive cats with new owners.
Although FIV and HIV are related, neither of the two viruses can infect the other's species.

teile.einleitung: A fish ladder is a structure that lets fish get past an obstacle in a river, such as a weir or a power station. Instead of a high wall, they find many small steps there or a natural side stream. In this way lake trout, salmon or eels can migrate upstream again.
wichtigste: Fish ladders help fish to get past weirs, dams and steps.
Many fish migrate upstream to their spawning grounds.
Weirs and dams block lake trout from reaching their spawning streams.
A fish ladder often consists of many small pools one behind the other.
There are also natural bypass streams and even fish lifts.
Fish ladders help salmon, trout, eels and many other species.
In Switzerland, obstacles in rivers have to be gradually made passable again.

abschnitte.text: A **fish ladder**, also called a **fish pass**, is a channel of water beside an obstacle in a river. It divides the difference in height into many small steps. Each step is only so high that a fish can manage it with a leap or powerful swimming. Between the steps lie calmer pools in which the fish can rest. In this way they get upwards step by step.

Many fish have to migrate in order to spawn or find food. The **lake trout**, for example, goes from the lake up into the streams, where it lays its eggs. **Weirs**, dams and power stations block its way. In Switzerland there are tens of thousands of such artificial obstacles in the waters. Without a fish ladder, the fish cannot reach their spawning grounds, and the population collapses.

In a **pool pass**, the water flows through a series of pools separated by small walls. In a vertical slot pass, the fish swim through vertical slots from pool to pool. A **bypass channel** is a natural stream with stones and gravel that leads round the obstacle. At very high dams there are sometimes fish lifts or locks. It is always important that the entrance is easy to find, because fish follow the current.

Salmon and trout leap and swim powerfully against the current. Weaker swimmers such as bullheads or young fish need gentle steps and rough bottoms. Young eels even crawl across damp surfaces and use special eel passes with bristles. Good fish ladders are built so that as many as possible of the river's species can get through. Some installations have windows or counting pools in which experts count the fish.

On the High Rhine, for example at the Rheinfelden power station, large fish passes have been built. They are also meant to help bring the **salmon** back to Switzerland, where it disappeared around the middle of the 20th century. Since 2011, the Swiss **Water Protection Act** has required power stations to make fish migration possible again. The operators therefore have to modify their installations bit by bit. Migration downstream is also important, because fish must not get into the turbines.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another word for fish ladder.
A structure across a river that dams up the water.
A place where fish lay their eggs.
A natural stream that leads round an obstacle.

gewusst: The first simple fish ladders were built several hundred years ago.
In some fish ladders, cameras count every fish that swims through.
Salmon can leap more than three metres high at waterfalls.

teile.einleitung: Goose bumps are the small bumps that suddenly appear on our skin when we are cold or experience something exciting. The fine hairs stand on end as they do. The German name, Gänsehaut, literally “goose skin”, probably comes from the skin of a plucked goose.
wichtigste: Goose bumps appear when tiny muscles at the hair roots contract.
The hairs stand up and small bumps form around them.
You get goose bumps in the cold, but also with fear, joy or beautiful music.
The body controls them automatically, and you cannot trigger them at will.
The name probably comes from the skin of a plucked goose with small bumps.
In animals with thick fur, raising the hairs helps against the cold.
In humans, goose bumps are a leftover from earlier times.

abschnitte.text: **Goose bumps** are a reaction of our skin in which the hairs stand up and small dots become visible. They often show on the arms and legs, sometimes also on the neck. In medicine they are also called **cutis anserina**, which is Latin for goose skin. After a few seconds or minutes they disappear again by themselves.

At every hair root sits a tiny muscle called the **arrector pili**. In the cold or with strong feelings, the nervous system sends a signal, and these muscles contract. This makes the hair stand up, and the skin around the hair root bulges into a small bump. It is controlled by the **autonomic nervous system**, which works without our will, and by the stress hormone **adrenaline**.

In animals with thick fur, raising the hairs has a clear use. More air stays trapped between the raised hairs, which insulates like a warm blanket. In danger, an animal with bristling fur looks bigger and more dangerous, like a hissing cat with a fluffed-up tail. In humans, with their fine body hair, this hardly achieves anything any more. It is a leftover from **evolution**.

Many people get goose bumps when they hear music that moves them. They can also appear during an exciting film, a scary story or a great win in sport. Researchers suspect that reward areas in the **brain** are active when this happens. People then sometimes speak of a “goose bump moment”.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the name come from?
abschnitte.text: The name probably comes from the skin of a plucked goose. If you remove the feathers from a goose, you see small bumps in the places where the **feathers** sat. These resemble the little bumps on our skin. In English they are called “goose bumps” too, while in French people say “chair de poule”, that is, chicken skin.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny muscle at the hair root that makes the hair stand up.
An automatic reaction of the body that you do not control at will.
A hormone that the body releases in excitement or danger.
The slow change of living things over very many generations.

gewusst: A very few people can reportedly trigger goose bumps at will, but this is very rare.
Hedgehogs, too, raise their spines in danger using similar muscles.

teile.einleitung: A compound eye is an eye made up of many tiny individual eyes. Insects such as butterflies, flies, bees and ants see their surroundings with it. Each single eye supplies one small picture point, and together they form a picture like a mosaic.
wichtigste: A compound eye is made up of many tiny single eyes, called ommatidia.
It is also called a complex eye.
Insects and many crustaceans have compound eyes.
A butterfly's eyes can have thousands of facets.
Compound eyes are especially good at detecting movement.
Bees can see ultraviolet light, which is invisible to us.
A grasshopper has two large compound eyes.

abschnitte.text: A **compound eye** is made up of many tiny, six-sided single eyes called **ommatidia**. Each single eye has its own small lens and looks in a slightly different direction. The brain puts the many picture points together into one overall picture. Experts also call it a **complex eye**.

The number of facets varies greatly from animal to animal. Ants often have only a few hundred facets, and some workers even fewer. A butterfly's eyes can have thousands of facets, and in large dragonflies there are around 30,000 per eye. The more facets, the sharper the picture usually is.

Compound eyes do not see as sharply as our eyes, but they are especially good at detecting movement. A fly therefore notices straight away when a hand comes near. Butterflies can detect movement and colours especially well with their compound eyes. Bees can even see **ultraviolet light**, and so they find patterns on flowers that are invisible to us.

A grasshopper has two large compound eyes at the sides of its head. Ants also see their surroundings with compound eyes, but they rely heavily on their sense of smell. Many insects also have small **simple eyes** on the forehead, which mainly tell light from dark. Crustaceans such as crabs and shrimps also have compound eyes.

Compound eyes have existed on Earth for a very long time. The **trilobites**, extinct sea animals, already had such eyes over 500 million years ago. Their fossilised eyes can still be recognised in fossils today. Researchers are now building tiny cameras modelled on the compound eye.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single small eye within a compound eye.
A transparent part of the eye that focuses light.
Light that people cannot see but bees can.
Small, simple eyes on the forehead of many insects.

gewusst: Because flies perceive many more images per second than we do, an approaching fly swatter looks to them as if it were in slow motion.
A dragonfly's large compound eyes cover almost its whole head.

teile.einleitung: The adipose fin is a small, soft fin on the back of some fish, between the dorsal fin and the tail fin. It is typical of salmon-like fish such as trout, salmon and whitefish. For a long time it was thought to be useless, but today more is known about its job.
wichtigste: The adipose fin sits between the dorsal fin and the tail fin.
It has no fin rays and is soft and fleshy.
It is typical of salmon-like fish such as salmon, trout, lake trout and whitefish.
Many catfish and characins also have an adipose fin.
Researchers suspect that it helps to sense currents in the water.
In Switzerland, many salmon-like fish are easy to recognise by their adipose fin.

abschnitte.text: The adipose fin is a small, rounded fin at the back of the back. Unlike the other fins, it has no supporting **fin rays**. It is made of skin, connective tissue and sometimes a little fat, which is where its name comes from. Fish cannot raise or move it themselves.

The adipose fin is best known in the **salmon-like fish**. These include salmon, brown trout, lake trout, Arctic char, grayling and whitefish. Many catfish, the colourful **characins** from the aquarium and some deep-sea fish also have one. Altogether it occurs in several thousand species of fish.

For a long time people believed the adipose fin was a useless leftover from the past. Research has shown, however, that many **nerves** run through it. It is thought to work like a sensor and to help fish to sense eddies in the water. In this way they can swim better in flowing streams.

In some countries, fish farmers cut off the adipose fin of young salmon before they are released. In this way you can later tell whether a caught fish comes from a **farm** or grew up wild. This marking is quick to do and easy to see. Today, because of the fin's possible importance, it is also discussed critically.

In Swiss lakes and rivers, many fish with an adipose fin live. The **whitefish** are the most important food fish for professional fishers in many lakes. Lake trout, brown trout and grayling also belong to them. Anyone who spots a small fin between the back and the tail while fishing very probably has a salmon-like fish on the hook.

begriffe.erklaerung: Thin, supporting rods that spread out most fins.
A family of fish that includes salmon, trout, char and whitefish.
Silvery salmon-like fish that are often caught in Swiss lakes.
Small, often colourful fish that many people keep in aquariums.

gewusst: The adipose fin can help to identify fish species at a glance.
In salmon, it has been found that animals without an adipose fin beat their tails harder in a current.
Depending on the region, whitefish in Switzerland are also called Albeli, Balchen or Blaufelchen.

teile.einleitung: In everyday life “fit” means sporty and healthy, but in biology the word has a different meaning. There, fitness describes how successfully a living thing has offspring that themselves survive and reproduce. This idea is a key to understanding evolution.
wichtigste: Biological fitness is the ability to produce offspring successfully and to secure their survival.
In biology, fitness does not mean strong or sporty.
Animals with high fitness pass on their features to more offspring.
This is the core of natural selection according to Charles Darwin.
Fitness always depends on the environment in which an animal lives.
Helping relatives can also raise fitness.
The expression “survival of the fittest” comes from Herbert Spencer.

abschnitte.text: In **evolutionary biology**, **fitness** describes how many offspring that can survive a living thing has compared with others of its species. An animal with many young that themselves grow up and reproduce has a high fitness. An animal that leaves no offspring has a fitness of zero, no matter how strong it is. Fitness therefore measures reproductive success. It is always a comparison between individuals of the same species.

The English naturalist **Charles Darwin** described **natural selection** in 1859. Living things that are better adapted to their environment have, on average, more offspring. Their features are therefore passed on more often to the next generation. Over many generations, whole species change in this way. The philosopher Herbert Spencer coined the expression “survival of the fittest” for this, which means more “survival of the best adapted” than “of the strongest”.

A feature is not equally useful everywhere. A thick coat is an advantage for a mountain hare in the Alps, but in the desert it would be a hindrance. A white winter coat camouflages in snow, but on brown ground it gives the animal away. If the environment changes, for example through **climate change**, the advantages can also shift. That is why there is no “fittest” animal in general.

The peacock has a magnificent tail that actually hinders it and attracts enemies. But because females prefer males with beautiful tails, these have more offspring. This is called **sexual selection**. A rabbit that has many litters a year can achieve a high fitness even if many young are eaten. An elephant has only a few young but looks after them for a long time and intensively.

Workers among honeybees have no offspring of their own. Even so, they contribute to passing on their genes, because they support their sisters and the queen. The biologist William D. Hamilton explained this in 1964 with **inclusive fitness**. It counts not only one's own young but also the success of close relatives. This explains why some animals help others.

begriffe.erklaerung: Slow change of living things over many generations.
Better adapted living things have more offspring and pass on their features.
Reproductive success including help given to relatives.
Selection through the choice of a mate, for example when females prefer attractive males.

gewusst: A healthy, strong stag with no offspring has, biologically speaking, a lower fitness than a weakly one with many young.
Darwin used the expression “survival of the fittest” only in later editions of his famous book.
In bees, a worker can pass on her genes through her sisters without laying eggs herself.

teile.einleitung: The Eurasian otter is a skilful swimmer from the mustelid family that lives on rivers and lakes. It had almost completely disappeared from Switzerland and is now slowly returning. Anyone who sees a wild otter is very lucky.
wichtigste: The Eurasian otter is a mustelid that lives in and beside water.
Its brown fur is very dense and keeps it warm and dry when diving.
It eats mainly fish, while the beaver, by contrast, eats plants.
When diving, it can close its nose and ears.
The mother usually has two to three young once a year.
In the 20th century, the otter was almost completely wiped out in Switzerland.
Today it is regarded as a symbol of clean, healthy waters.

abschnitte.text: The **Eurasian otter** grows to about 60 to 90 centimetres long without its tail, and a powerful tail of around 30 to 45 centimetres is added to that. It usually weighs between 6 and 12 kilograms. Its body is long and streamlined, and its paws have **webbing**. The brown fur is extremely dense, and air stays trapped between the hairs, which insulates it. When diving, its nose and ears close, and with its long whiskers it senses prey in murky water.

Otters live on rivers, streams, lakes and marshes with natural banks. Clean water, enough fish and hiding places under roots or in bushes are important. Their den is called a **holt**, and the entrance is often under water. An otter's territory stretches along a river and can be several kilometres long. Otters are out and about mainly at dusk and at night.

The otter eats mainly fish, for example perch, trout or white fish. It also catches crayfish, frogs, waterbirds and small mammals. A grown otter needs about a kilogram of food a day. In this it differs clearly from the **beaver**, which eats only plants such as bark, twigs and herbs. Otters hunt alone and are very agile divers.

The otter mother usually has young once a year, often two to three. The young are born blind and have to learn to swim. They stay with their mother for about a year before they look for a territory of their own. Otters are very playful. They like to slide into the water on mud slides or, in winter, on snow.

In the past the otter was regarded as a competitor of fishers and was hunted heavily. In addition there were polluted waters and straightened rivers. It has been protected in Switzerland since 1952, but it still almost completely disappeared, and in 1989 it was considered extinct. Since about 2009, otters have been moving in from Austria along the Inn into the Engadine, and later they also turned up on the Aare and the Rhine. It is regarded as an **indicator species** for intact waters, because it can only live where the water is clean and has enough fish.

begriffe.erklaerung: A family of predators with a long, slim body that also includes the badger and the weasel.
The otter's den, often with an entrance under water.
An area that an animal lives in and defends against others of its species.
A species whose presence shows that a habitat is healthy.

gewusst: The otter's fur is among the densest in the animal kingdom, with tens of thousands of hairs growing on one square centimetre.
Otters mark their territory with droppings that, surprisingly, are said to smell a little of jasmine or fish.
Young otters are at first afraid of the water and are sometimes pushed in by their mother.

teile.einleitung: The scarlet darter is a dragonfly whose males are a bright, fiery red. Originally it was at home mainly around the Mediterranean. Because it is getting warmer, it is spreading ever further north and can now also be seen in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The scarlet darter is a bright red dragonfly.
Its scientific name is Crocothemis erythraea.
Only the males are fiery red, the females are yellowish brown.
It belongs to the darters.
It loves warm, sunny ponds and pools.
Its larvae live in the water and hunt small animals there.
It has spread northwards with climate warming.

abschnitte.text: The scarlet darter grows to about 3.5 to 4.5 centimetres long. The males have a broad, flat abdomen that is **bright red**, and even the wing veins shimmer reddish. The females, by contrast, are **yellowish brown** and much less conspicuous. At the base of the wings, both have a small amber-coloured spot.

The scarlet darter occurs in Africa, southern Europe and parts of Asia. It likes warm, shallow, sunny **still waters** such as ponds, pools and gravel pits. In recent decades it has spread strongly northwards because of **climate warming**. In Switzerland it is now found mainly at lower, warm altitudes at many bodies of water.

Scarlet darters are skilful **hunters on the wing**. They catch mosquitoes, flies and other small insects in mid-air. With their huge compound eyes they can see almost all round. The males like to sit on a lookout post on the bank and set off from there on short hunting flights.

The males defend a small **territory** by the water and drive off rivals. After mating, the female dips her abdomen into the water and lays the eggs as she does so. From these hatch **larvae**, which live in the water and eat small water animals. After several moults, the larva climbs up a stalk and the finished dragonfly emerges.

The scarlet darter is regarded as an example of how climate change is altering the animal world. Experts follow its spread closely. It is completely harmless to people, since dragonflies do not sting. Anyone who visits a warm pond in summer can, with a bit of luck, watch it well.

begriffe.erklaerung: A family of dragonflies that includes many colourful species with a broad abdomen.
The young form of an insect, which looks different from the adult animal.
Bodies of water without a current, for example ponds and pools.
An area that an animal defends against others of its species.

gewusst: Dragonflies have existed for over 300 million years, much longer than the dinosaurs.
The scientific name erythraea means roughly “the red one”.
Dragonflies can move their four wings independently of one another and can even fly backwards.

teile.einleitung: Carnivores are animals that feed wholly or mainly on other animals. Experts call them carnivores, from the Latin word for meat. From the tiny ladybird to the polar bear, there are carnivores of all sizes.
wichtigste: A carnivore feeds on other animals.
Animals that eat almost nothing but meat are called carnivores.
Pointed canine teeth and sharp carnassial teeth are typical.
Cats are strict carnivores, while dogs and bears also eat plants.
Carnivores are often far up the food chain.
There are even carnivorous plants such as the sundew.
In Switzerland live carnivores such as the lynx, wolf, fox and stoat.

abschnitte.text: A **carnivore** is an animal that feeds on other animals. The opposite is the **herbivore** such as cows and deer. Animals that eat both, such as wild boar, bears or humans, are called **omnivores**. Carnivores hunt their prey themselves, or they eat dead animals, and then they are called scavengers. They include mammals, birds, reptiles, fish, insects and spiders.

Meat-eating mammals usually have long, pointed **canine teeth** for seizing and sharp **carnassial teeth** that cut meat like scissors. Many have claws, a good sense of smell and forward-facing eyes to judge distances well. Their gut is shorter than in herbivores, because meat is easier to digest. Birds of prey such as the golden eagle have sharp talons and a hooked beak. Snakes swallow their prey whole.

**Cats** are strict carnivores, they need certain nutrients that occur only in meat. Wolves and foxes eat mainly meat, but also berries and fruit.
