The group of **carnivorans** in biology is also called Carnivora, but not all of them eat meat. The giant panda belongs to it and eats almost nothing but bamboo. Conversely, there are many meat-eaters that are not carnivorans, for example dragonflies or sharks.

Carnivores stand higher up in the **food chain** than herbivores. The fox eats the mouse, the mouse eats seeds. At the very top are apex predators such as the wolf, lynx, orca or polar bear, which have hardly any natural enemies. Carnivores regulate the number of their prey animals and so maintain the balance in nature. The lynx in the Swiss Alps and the Jura hunts mainly roe deer and chamois.

A few plants also catch animals. The **sundew** grows in Swiss bogs and catches insects with sticky drops on its leaves. The butterwort also uses sticky leaves. The Venus flytrap from North America snaps its leaves shut in a flash. Such plants mostly grow on soils poor in nutrients and in this way obtain extra nutrients.

begriffe.erklaerung: Technical word for a meat-eater.
A sharp cheek tooth that cuts meat like scissors.
An animal that eats both plants and animals.
A series that shows who eats whom.

gewusst: The giant panda belongs to the carnivorans but eats almost nothing but bamboo.
A ladybird is a carnivore and can eat thousands of aphids in its life.
A wolf can eat several kilograms of meat in a single meal.

teile.einleitung: In German, walking “im Gänsemarsch”, literally “in goose march”, means walking one behind the other in a line. The expression comes from geese, which often walk neatly one after another. People, too, walk in single file on narrow paths or in groups.
wichtigste: Walking “im Gänsemarsch” means walking one behind the other in a line.
The expression comes from goose families, which often waddle in a line.
Usually an experienced animal goes at the front and the others follow.
On narrow mountain paths you walk in single file for safety.
Nursery and school classes also often walk in single file.
Many other animals such as ducks, elephants or ants also move in lines.
In the air, wild geese often fly in a V formation.

abschnitte.text: The German **Gänsemarsch** is an idiom and means that several people walk one behind the other in a single line. The expression comes from geese, which often walk neatly one behind the other. Goose families with their chicks in particular move along like this. A similar German expression is “im Entenmarsch”, literally “in duck march”, and in English you say “in single file”.

abschnitte.titel: Why do geese walk in a line?
abschnitte.text: Young geese, the **goslings**, follow their mother from the very first day. After hatching they have imprinted on her and stay close behind her. This way they do not lose each other and are better protected. Often one parent goes at the front and the gander at the back, to watch for dangers.

On narrow **mountain paths** in the Alps you walk in single file so that nobody slips off the side of the path. The person with the most experience often goes at the front and sets the pace. Whoever goes at the back makes sure that nobody is left behind. On glaciers, too, rope teams walk in a line, joined by a **rope**.

Nursery and school classes often walk in single file on outings so that the teacher can see everyone. In Switzerland the rule is that where there is no **pavement**, pedestrians walk at the edge of the road. Outside built-up areas you walk on the left edge, so that you can see the cars coming towards you. A group is then safest walking one behind the other in single file.

It is not only geese that walk one behind the other. Elephants often travel in a long line across the savannah, and ants follow a scent trail along **ant trails**. The caterpillars of the **processionary moth** crawl head to tail in long chains. In the air, wild geese fly in a V formation, with each goose benefiting from the updraught of the one in front.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fixed group of words with a figurative meaning.
When a young animal binds itself firmly to a particular creature shortly after birth.
Mountaineers who are joined by a rope for safety.
The raised footpath beside the road, called “Bürgersteig” in Germany.

gewusst: By flying in a V formation, wild geese save energy and can cover longer distances.
Processionary moths have their name because their caterpillars travel in long lines as in a procession.

teile.einleitung: The Galapagos penguin is a very special penguin, because it lives not in the ice but on warm islands on the equator. It is the penguin species that lives furthest north. Sadly, it is also one of the rarest penguins in the world.
wichtigste: The Galapagos penguin lives on the Galapagos Islands in the Pacific, which belong to Ecuador.
It is the penguin species that lives furthest north, even close to the equator.
Unlike many other penguins, it lives not in Antarctica but on warm islands.
It is only about 50 centimetres tall and is one of the smallest penguins.
Cold ocean currents bring it enough fish to eat.
It is considered endangered.
There are only a few thousand animals left, or even fewer.

abschnitte.text: The Galapagos penguin is about 50 centimetres tall and weighs around 2 to 2.5 kilograms. Its back is black, its belly white, and a narrow white band runs across its face. It belongs to the genus of **banded penguins**, which also includes the Humboldt penguin. Like all penguins, it cannot fly, but it is an excellent swimmer.

The **Galapagos Islands** lie in the Pacific about 1,000 kilometres off the coast of Ecuador. Most Galapagos penguins live on the western islands of Isabela and Fernandina. A few animals even live just north of the **equator**, which no other penguin species manages. This is possible because cold ocean currents such as the **Humboldt Current** bring cool, nutrient-rich water.

Galapagos penguins eat small shoaling fish such as sardines and anchovies. They hunt mostly by day near the coast and dive quickly through the shoals of fish. They often hunt in small groups. Because they live close to their feeding grounds, they usually return to land every evening.

On the hot lava rocks the penguins have to protect themselves from overheating. They pant like a dog, look for shade and hold their flippers over their feet to protect them from the sun. They lay their eggs in cool **caves** and rock crevices. When it gets too hot, they go into the water to cool down.

On the Red List, the Galapagos penguin is considered **endangered**. Particularly dangerous is the weather phenomenon **El Niño**, in which the sea warms up and many fish disappear. In such years many penguins starve. The Galapagos Islands are now a national park, and researchers even build artificial nesting caves for the penguins.

begriffe.erklaerung: The imaginary line around the middle of the Earth that divides it into a northern and a southern half.
A stream in the sea that carries water over long distances.
A weather phenomenon in which the Pacific warms up unusually strongly.
A large protected area in which nature is especially protected.

gewusst: The Galapagos Islands became famous because the naturalist Charles Darwin observed animals there in 1835.
Galapagos penguins can breed several times a year if there is enough food.

teile.einleitung: Falconry is hunting with trained birds of prey such as falcons, goshawks or eagles. It is one of the oldest forms of hunting in the world and is still practised today. A falconer lives closely with his or her bird, and this takes a lot of patience and knowledge.
wichtigste: In falconry, people hunt with trained birds of prey.
The peregrine falcon has been especially prized for falconry for centuries.
Falconry is several thousand years old and probably comes from Asia.
Important equipment includes a leather glove, a hood and jesses.
Since 2010, falconry has been part of UNESCO's intangible cultural heritage.
Today falconers also use their birds to drive away troublesome birds, for example at airports.

abschnitte.text: A **falconer** raises a bird of prey and trains it to hunt prey and then return. The bird remains a wild animal, and does not become obedient like a dog. It comes back because it is sure to get food from the falconer. The training takes time every day and a lot of trust between person and bird.

Falconry probably arose several thousand years ago on the steppes of Asia. In the Middle Ages it was a popular pastime of kings and nobles in Europe. The Hohenstaufen emperor **Frederick II** wrote a famous book about hunting with birds in the 13th century. In the Arab world and in Central Asia, falconry is still very important today.

The **peregrine falcon** has always been especially sought after because of its speed. In a dive it can reach over 300 kilometres per hour. For hunting in the forest, falconers like to use the goshawk, and in Mongolia riders even hunt with the golden eagle. The Harris's hawk is also very popular today, because it hunts well as part of a team.

The falconer wears a thick **leather glove** so that the sharp talons do not hurt. A small leather cap, the **hood**, covers the bird's eyes and calms it. On its legs the bird wears leather straps by which it can be held. It often also has a little bell or a small transmitter so that it can be found again.

Today falconry is not only hunting but also nature conservation and education. At airports, birds of prey drive away other birds so that there are no dangerous collisions with aircraft. At flying displays, visitors learn a lot about birds of prey. Since 2010, UNESCO has counted falconry as **intangible cultural heritage**. In Switzerland, a permit is needed to keep birds of prey, and animal welfare is strictly regulated.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person who keeps and trains birds of prey and hunts with them.
A bird with sharp talons and a hooked beak that hunts other animals.
A leather cap over the bird's eyes that keeps it calm.
Customs and skills that are protected as a valuable heritage of humanity.

gewusst: Many words such as “Beizjagd” (hawking) come from the old language of falconers.
In some Gulf states, falcons even have their own passports for air travel.
In a dive, the peregrine falcon is considered the fastest animal in the world.

teile.einleitung: An exuvia is the empty shell that an animal leaves behind when it moults. The exuviae of dragonflies are especially well known: they stay hanging on reed stems after the dragonfly has emerged. They look like the animal itself, but they are empty and light as a feather.
wichtigste: An exuvia is the empty larval shell that remains after hatching.
It is produced when animals with an outer skeleton moult.
Dragonflies often leave their exuviae on reeds and plant stems.
Spiders, grasshoppers, cicadas and crustaceans also leave exuviae.
In snakes, people speak of the shed skin or the slough.
Researchers use exuviae to work out which species live in a body of water.

abschnitte.text: The word **exuvia** comes from the Latin word for “clothing taken off”. It means the empty shell that an animal leaves behind after **moulting**. It has exactly the shape of the animal, with legs, head and even eyes. Inside, however, it is hollow and very light.

Insects, spiders and crustaceans have a hard outer skeleton that does not grow with them. When the animal gets bigger, a new, soft skin forms underneath. Then the old shell usually splits open along the back, and the animal pulls itself out. The exuvia stays behind, while the new skin hardens within hours.

Dragonfly larvae live in the water for one or several years. To emerge, they climb out of the water on a reed stem or stalk. There the larval skin tears open, and the finished dragonfly squeezes out and pumps up its wings. The empty **larval shell** often stays hanging on the stem for weeks.

Exuviae are very useful for researchers. From them you can tell which **dragonfly species** have developed in a pond without disturbing any animal. In Switzerland, experts collect exuviae to monitor rare species. Because an exuvia shows that the larva has successfully left the water, it proves that the species breeds there.

Cicadas also leave striking exuviae, which stick to tree trunks. Spiders moult several times in their lives, and their shells can be found in webs or corners. Snakes and lizards also moult, and a snake's shed skin is also called a **slough**. Crustaceans such as the freshwater crayfish even cast off their whole hard shell.

begriffe.erklaerung: Shedding the old skin or shell that has become too small.
A young animal that still looks different from the adult.
A hard shell on the outside of the body that gives support.
The shed skin of a snake.

gewusst: A dragonfly exuvia even shows the extendable mask with which the larva seized its prey under water.
Depending on the species, spiders moult several times before they are adult.

teile.einleitung: The lowland tapir is a large mammal from South America with a short, flexible trunk. Although it looks a bit like a pig, it is related to horses and rhinoceroses. It is regarded as the largest native land mammal of South America.
wichtigste: The lowland tapir lives in the forests and wetlands of South America.
It has a short, flexible trunk-like nose with which it grasps leaves.
Tapirs are odd-toed ungulates and related to horses and rhinoceroses.
The lowland tapir eats only plants, mainly leaves and fruit.
It is a good swimmer and likes to flee into the water.
Its enemies include the jaguar and the puma.
The species is considered vulnerable.

abschnitte.text: The **lowland tapir** grows to about two metres long and around one metre high, and can weigh over 200 kilograms. Its fur is short and dark brown to grey. On its neck it has a short, bristly mane. The upper lip and the nose are drawn out into a short **trunk**, which is very flexible. It has four toes on the front feet and three on the hind feet, each with a small hoof.

The lowland tapir lives in large parts of tropical South America, from the north as far as Argentina and Paraguay. It inhabits rainforests, wet savannas and swamps, preferably near water. It is especially widespread in the **Amazon region**. It is out and about mainly at night and at dusk. Real tapir paths form along its routes through the forest.

Tapirs are pure **plant-eaters**. With their trunk they pick leaves, shoots, water plants and fallen fruit. Many seeds pass out again undigested. In this way they spread plants over long distances, which is why they are also called “gardeners of the forest”. As a supplement, they visit salt licks to take in minerals.

Tapirs usually live as **loners**. They swim and dive excellently and flee into the water when in danger. Their greatest natural enemy is the **jaguar**, along with the puma and large crocodiles. After a pregnancy of about 13 months, the female usually gives birth to a single young one. The young animal has brown fur with pale stripes and spots, which camouflages it in the forest like a watermelon.

The lowland tapir is classed as **vulnerable** by the International Union for Conservation of Nature. Its forests are cleared for pastures, fields and roads. It is also hunted for its meat. Because a female has a young one only every two years, populations recover only slowly. Protected areas and breeding programmes in zoos, including in Europe, help the species.

begriffe.erklaerung: Mammals with an odd number of weight-bearing toes, such as the horse, rhinoceros and tapir.
An elongated, flexible nose with which an animal can grasp.
An animal that mostly lives alone.
A spot with salty ground where animals take in minerals.

gewusst: Tapirs have existed for many millions of years and have hardly changed, so they are regarded as living fossils.
A tapir can move along the bottom of a body of water under water and use its trunk like a snorkel.
Young tapirs lose their stripes after about half a year.

teile.einleitung: The brown hare is a fast long-distance runner that lives in open fields and meadows. With its long ears and powerful hind legs it is easy to recognise. Although it looks similar to the rabbit, it is a species in its own right with a different way of life.
wichtigste: The brown hare lives in fields, meadows and at the edge of woods.
It can run at up to about 70 kilometres per hour.
Young hares are born furry and with their eyes open, young rabbits naked and blind.
Brown hares do not dig burrows but rest in a shallow hollow, the form.
Hares are plant-eaters and are not rodents but lagomorphs.
In Switzerland, numbers have fallen sharply since the 1970s.

abschnitte.text: The brown hare is larger than a wild rabbit and usually weighs about 3.5 to 5 kilograms. Its fur is earth-brown to yellowish grey, and the belly is pale. Striking features are the long **ears** with black tips and the long hind legs. Its eyes sit at the sides of its head, so it can see almost all round and notices enemies early.

Brown hares love open landscapes with meadows, fields, hedges and fallow land. It is widespread in Europe, and originally it comes from the steppes. It spends the day crouched in a shallow hollow, the **form**. When in danger, it first lies still and only runs away at the last moment.

The brown hare eats grasses, herbs, clover, buds and, in winter, bark as well. It is mainly active at dusk and at night. When fleeing, it makes lightning-fast **zigzags**, so that a fox or dog has trouble catching it. In spring the hares chase one another and even box on their hind legs, usually a female fending off a male who is too pushy.

A female hare usually has three or four litters a year, each with one to five young. The young are **precocial**: they are born furry and with their eyes open. The mother leaves them alone during the day and suckles them only about once a day, so that no enemies notice them. Anyone who finds a single young hare should therefore definitely leave it where it is.

In Switzerland there are far fewer brown hares today than in the past. The reasons are intensive **agriculture**, fast mowing machines, roads and a lack of hedges and fallow land. Many young hares also die in wet, cold weather. With **flower-rich fallow strips**, hedges and lightly fertilised meadows, people are trying to give them more habitat again.

begriffe.erklaerung: A shallow hollow in the ground in which the hare rests.
Young animals that can see and move soon after birth.
Sudden changes of direction while fleeing.
A strip at the edge of a field with wild flowers that offers animals shelter and food.

gewusst: A brown hare can leap more than two metres from a standing start.
Hares eat some of their droppings a second time, to get more nutrients out of their food.
The Easter bunny is an old custom that has been known in Switzerland and Germany for centuries.

teile.einleitung: The Gamsbart, or chamois beard, is a traditional hat decoration from the Alpine region. It looks like a bushy brush and is tied from the long back hairs of the chamois. It is part of many traditional costumes, above all in Bavaria and Austria.
wichtigste: The Gamsbart is made from the long back hair of the chamois.
Despite its name, it comes not from the chin but from the back of the animal.
The best hairs come from male chamois in their winter coat.
The hairs are tied into a bushy tuft in a small sleeve.
The Gamsbart is worn at the side or back of a traditional hat.
A large, fine Gamsbart needs hair from several chamois and can be very expensive.
It is found mainly in Bavaria, Austria and South Tyrol.

abschnitte.text: The **Gamsbart** is a tuft of animal hair that is worn as a decoration on a hat. It is usually fixed to traditional hats or hunters' hats. The name is somewhat misleading, because the hairs do not grow on the chamois's chin. They come from a stripe of hair on the back, which is called the **dorsal stripe**.

abschnitte.titel: Where do the hairs come from?
abschnitte.text: In winter the **chamois** grows particularly long hairs on its back, often over 10 centimetres long. They are longest and finest on older bucks. The hairs often have pale tips, which are called **frost**. The more pale tips a Gamsbart has, the more valuable it is.

A Gamsbart is tied by hand, which is an old craft. The hairs are sorted, cleaned and tied together so that the tips fan out nicely. At the lower end they are held in a small metal **sleeve**. For a large Gamsbart you need hair from several animals, and the work can take many hours.

The Gamsbart is a well-known sign of folk culture, above all in **Bavaria**, Austria and South Tyrol. It is part of many traditional costumes there and is worn at festivals, parades and celebrations. Originally it was also a sign of successful hunters. Besides the Gamsbart there are also hat decorations made of deer hair or **badger hair**.

In Switzerland, too, many chamois live, above all in the Alps and in the Jura. They are hunted in the hunting season in autumn under strict rules so that the population stays healthy. In Switzerland the Gamsbart is less common than in Bavaria and Austria, but you can see it on some hunters' hats. The hairs come from animals that were shot during the **hunt**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Traditional clothing of a region that is worn at festivals.
A dark stripe of hair that runs along the back of some animals.
The male of chamois, roe deer or goats.
A small tube in which something is held.

gewusst: Particularly large and fine Gamsbärte can cost several thousand francs.
The hairs for a Gamsbart have to be taken in winter, because the summer coat is much shorter.

teile.einleitung: The African wildcat is a small wildcat that lives in Africa and the Middle East. It is the ancestor of our domestic cats. Anyone who knows a tabby house cat can easily imagine what an African wildcat looks like.
wichtigste: The African wildcat has the scientific name Felis silvestris lybica or, in the newer classification, Felis lybica.
The domestic cat probably descends from the African wildcat.
It lives in Africa, on the Arabian Peninsula and in the Middle East.
Its fur is sandy to greyish brown with fine stripes.
It hunts mainly mice and other small animals.
As long as 10,000 years ago, wildcats began to live near people.

abschnitte.text: The African wildcat is somewhat larger and slimmer than many house cats. It usually weighs about 3 to 6 kilograms. Its **fur** is pale sandy, grey or yellowish brown and has faint dark stripes. Long legs and the reddish backs of the ears are typical.

African wildcats live in savannas, steppes, scrubland and at the edge of deserts. They are found in large parts of Africa, on the **Arabian Peninsula** and in the Middle East. They avoid dense rainforests and completely dry sandy deserts. During the day they hide in caves, rock crevices or dense bushes.

African wildcats are **ambush hunters**, which creep up and pounce in a flash. Their main prey is mice, rats and other small rodents. They also eat birds, lizards and large insects. They mostly hunt at dusk and at night.

abschnitte.titel: From wild animal to house cat
abschnitte.text: When people in the **Fertile Crescent** settled down and stored grain, the stores attracted many mice. The mice in turn attracted wildcats, which in this way came close to people. On Cyprus, researchers found a grave about 9,500 years old in which a person had been buried together with a cat. Later, in ancient Egypt, cats were greatly honoured and even linked with the goddess **Bastet**.

The African wildcat is widespread and is not considered threatened overall. One problem is that it mates with feral house cats, so that **hybrids** appear. No African wildcat lives in Switzerland, but its close relative, the **European wildcat**, does. This has become native again mainly in the Jura and also looks very similar to a house cat.

begriffe.erklaerung: A cat that lives freely in nature and was never tamed by people.
The long process by which wild animals become domestic animals.
An animal that waits quietly or creeps up and then suddenly pounces.
A cross between two different species or forms.

gewusst: All the house cats in the world, from the Siamese to the Persian, have the African wildcat as an ancestor.
Unlike dogs, cats were probably not deliberately tamed but came to people of their own accord.
In ancient Egypt, some cats were even mummified after their death.

teile.einleitung: Many fish do not stay in the same place all their lives but migrate, sometimes thousands of kilometres. They travel to streams, to the sea or to the river where they were born in order to spawn. Such fish are called migratory fish, and the lake trout is an example from Switzerland.
wichtigste: In fish migration, fish move back and forth between different habitats.
Most migrate in order to spawn, that is, to lay their eggs.
The lake trout migrates from the lake into the streams and is therefore a migratory fish.
Salmon migrate from the sea into rivers to spawn there.
Eels do the opposite and swim far out into the sea to spawn.
Migratory fish find their way with their sense of smell and other senses.
Weirs and power stations are a big problem for migratory fish.

abschnitte.text: **Fish migration** is the name for the regular travelling of fish between different waters or parts of waters. Fish that do this are called **migratory fish**. They mostly migrate to spawn, to find food or to reach a sheltered winter spot. Some migrations are only a few kilometres long, others cross oceans. Almost every species of fish migrates some distance at some point in its life.

abschnitte.titel: Salmon: from the sea to the river
abschnitte.text: The **salmon** hatches in a river and migrates to the sea as a young fish. There it grows for a few years and becomes big and strong. Then it swims back into exactly the river in which it was born. It finds it mainly with its fine sense of smell. Fish that move from the sea into fresh water to spawn are called **anadromous**.

abschnitte.titel: Eel: from the river to the sea
abschnitte.text: The European **eel** does exactly the opposite. It grows up in rivers and lakes, including in Switzerland. To spawn, it swims thousands of kilometres to the **Sargasso Sea** in the Atlantic. The tiny larvae drift back to Europe with the Gulf Stream, which takes about one to three years. Fish that go to the sea to spawn are called catadromous.

Even inland, many fish migrate. The **lake trout** lives in the lake and in autumn climbs up into the feeder streams to spawn in the gravel. The grayling and the common nase move in spring to their spawning grounds in rivers. In the past, thousands of salmon swam up the Rhine every year as far as Basel and on into the Aare. Because of power stations and polluted water, the salmon disappeared from Switzerland around the middle of the 20th century.

Weirs, dams and power stations block the way for migratory fish. In the **turbines**, fish migrating downstream can be injured. That is why fish ladders, bypass streams and protective screens are built. Straightened rivers without gravel banks also deprive fish of spawning grounds. When rivers are freely passable again, many migratory fish return.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fish that regularly travels back and forth between different waters.
Laying and fertilising eggs in fish and amphibians.
Migrates from the sea into rivers to spawn, like the salmon.
Migrates from fresh water to the sea to spawn, like the eel.

gewusst: On its migration upstream, a salmon usually no longer eats anything and lives on its fat reserves.
Eels from Swiss waters cover a distance of more than 6,000 kilometres to the Sargasso Sea.
Salmon can smell their home river again even after years in the sea.

teile.einleitung: The tree sparrow is a small songbird and a close relative of the house sparrow, which we call the “Spatz”. You can recognise it by its chocolate-brown cap and the black spot on its white cheek. It prefers to live on the edge of villages and in orchards rather than in the middle of a town.
wichtigste: The tree sparrow is the smaller relative of the house sparrow.
The brown cap and a black cheek spot are typical.
In the tree sparrow, males and females look the same.
It breeds in tree holes, holes in walls and, gladly, in nest boxes.
It eats seeds and feeds its young with insects.
In Switzerland it lives mainly in orchards and on farms.

abschnitte.text: The tree sparrow is about 14 centimetres long and so somewhat smaller than the house sparrow. It has a **brown cap**, a white cheek with a black spot and a narrow white collar. Unlike the house sparrow, males and females look almost **the same**. Its call is a short, somewhat harder “tschet”.

The tree sparrow lives all over Europe and in large parts of Asia. It likes landscapes with **standard orchards**, hedges, fields and farms. In Asia, by contrast, it also lives in the middle of cities, where it takes on the role of our house sparrow. In Switzerland you find it mainly on the Central Plateau and at lower altitudes.

Adult tree sparrows eat mainly seeds of grasses, wild plants and cereals. In winter they like to pick up grain at feeding places. They feed their young, on the other hand, mainly on **insects**, caterpillars and spiders. They therefore need a landscape with plenty of insects.

The tree sparrow is a **hole-nester** and nests in old woodpecker holes, cracks in walls or nest boxes. A pair often raises two or three broods a year. Outside the breeding season, tree sparrows live in flocks, sometimes together with finches and house sparrows. They often bathe in dust together to look after their feathers.

In many European countries the tree sparrow has become rarer. The reasons are the loss of standard trees, hedges and **fallow land**, as well as fewer insects and wild plants. You can help it with **nest boxes** and nature-friendly gardens. Wild flower strips at the edge of fields also offer it seeds and insects.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird that builds its nest in a hollow, a hole or a box.
A family of small, sturdy songbirds that includes the house sparrow.
A fruit tree with a tall trunk, typical of old orchards.
Rolling in dust, with which birds look after their feathers.

gewusst: With the tree sparrow, you can hardly tell males and females apart.
In China in the 1950s, tree sparrows were killed in huge numbers as pests, after which insects multiplied strongly.
In winter, tree sparrows often use nest boxes as warm places to sleep.

teile.einleitung: The European perch, usually called Egli in Switzerland, is one of the best-known fish in the country. It has dark vertical stripes, red fins and a spiny dorsal fin. Fried perch fillets are among the most popular fish dishes in Switzerland.
wichtigste: In Switzerland the perch is called Egli, in Ticino Pesce persico and on Lake Constance Kretzer.
It has two dorsal fins, the front one carrying sharp spines.
Dark vertical stripes camouflage it among plants and branches.
It hunts mainly with its eyes.
Very young perch eat tiny zooplankton, large perch also eat smaller fish.
To spawn, it moves into shallow shore zones.
Pike, cormorant and otter are among its predators.

abschnitte.text: The **European perch** usually grows to 15 to 30 centimetres long, and large animals reach close to 50 centimetres. Its back is olive green, and the sides have five to nine dark **vertical stripes**. The pelvic and anal fins are strikingly orange to red. It has two **dorsal fins**, the front one with sharp spiny rays and a dark spot at the end. When in danger, the perch raises this fin with its spines sticking out, so that a predator finds it hard to swallow.

The European perch lives in lakes, slow-flowing rivers and ponds in almost all of Europe and parts of Asia. In Switzerland it occurs in practically all the larger lakes, for example Lake Geneva, Lake Constance, Lake Zurich and Lake Neuchâtel. Here it is mostly called **Egli**, in Ticino Pesce persico and in French-speaking Switzerland perche. Around Lake Constance it is also called **Kretzer**. In winter it stays in deeper water and is less active.

Very young perch eat tiny **zooplankton**, that is, small crustaceans in the water. Later insect larvae, worms and crayfish are added. Large perch hunt small fish and sometimes even eat smaller perch of their own species. The perch tracks down its prey mainly with its eyes, so it hunts by day. Young perch swim in shoals, large ones often in small groups or alone.

In spring the perch move into shallow **shore zones** to spawn. The female lays her eggs in long, transparent **egg ribbons**, which she wraps around water plants, branches or stones. Such a ribbon can be over a metre long and contain tens of thousands of eggs. The perch's enemies are pike, pikeperch, cormorant, great crested grebe and otter. The vertical stripes help it to hide among plants and branches.

**Perch fillets**, fried in butter or breaded, are a classic in Switzerland, especially at the lakes. Professional fishers mostly catch perch with nets, anglers with the rod. Catches vary greatly from year to year. Because Swiss catches come nowhere near meeting demand, a large share of perch fillets is imported. When buying, check the origin if you want perch from a Swiss lake.

begriffe.erklaerung: The Swiss name for the European perch.
A hard, pointed ray in a fin.
Tiny animals that float in the water.
A long, jelly-like ribbon in which the perch lays its eggs.

gewusst: The egg ribbon of a large female perch can be longer than a child is tall.
Experts can read the age of a perch from annual rings on scales or ear stones.
When a perch eats too many others of its own kind, it is called cannibalism, and in large perch this happens regularly.

teile.einleitung: A foal is a young horse, a baby horse. Soon after birth it stands on its long, wobbly legs and can soon run alongside its mother.
wichtigste: A baby horse is called a foal.
The mother of a foal is called a mare, the father a stallion.
A mare carries her foal in her belly for about eleven months.
Usually only a single foal is born.
After about an hour, a foal can stand and drink.
A foal recognises its mother by her smell and by staying close to the mare.
After the first year of life, a young horse is called a yearling.

abschnitte.text: A horse in its first year of life is called a **foal**. A male foal is called a colt, a female foal a filly. Young donkeys and ponies are also called foals. After its first birthday, the animal is called a **yearling**.

A mare carries her foal for about eleven months, which is roughly 340 days. Birth often takes place at night and usually lasts only a short time. After about an hour, the foal stands up and looks for its mother's udder. The first milk is called **colostrum** and protects the foal from disease with important defensive substances.

A foal recognises its mother by her smell and because it stays close to her all the time. The mare also sniffs her foal straight after birth and remembers its smell. This close bond is called **imprinting**. In the first weeks, the foal hardly moves away from the mare and follows her everywhere.

Foals have very long legs in relation to their bodies. Their legs are already almost as long at birth as in an adult horse, so that in the wild they can flee with the herd straight away. Instead of a long mane they often have short, fluffy hair and a bushy tail. After a few weeks the foal begins to nibble grass and hay, but still drinks milk for months.

At about six months, a foal is usually separated from its mother, which is called **weaning**. In Switzerland, especially many foals of the Freiberger breed (Franches-Montagnes) are born, above all in the Jura. At the Marché-Concours in Saignelégier, Freiberger horses are presented every year in August. A young horse is ridden only after a few years, when it is fully grown.

begriffe.erklaerung: A female horse, that is, the mother of a foal.
A male horse.
The very first milk after birth, which contains especially many protective substances.
When a foal no longer drinks from its mother and is separated from her.

gewusst: Foals are born with soft pads on the hooves, so that they do not hurt the mother during birth.
Foals play a lot with one another and in doing so practise running, rearing and fighting.

teile.einleitung: Eusociality is the most highly developed form of living together in the animal kingdom. The animals live in one large colony in which the work is divided up and usually only one queen has offspring. Well-known examples are honeybees, ants and termites.
wichtigste: Eusociality is a form of society with a division of labour.
Usually only one queen is able to reproduce.
The other animals look after the young together.
Several generations live together in the colony.
Honeybees, ants, termites and bumblebees, for example, live in a eusocial way.
One mammal, the naked mole-rat, also lives in a eusocial way.
A eusocial colony works rather like one single large organism.

abschnitte.text: The word **eusociality** means roughly “true social life”. Experts use it when three features come together. First, many animals look after the young together. Second, several **generations** live together, and third, reproduction is divided up so that only a few animals have offspring.

In honeybees, only the **queen** lays eggs, sometimes more than a thousand in one day. The **workers** are also females, but as a rule they have no young of their own. They clean the combs, feed the larvae, build, guard the entrance and collect nectar and pollen. The males, the drones, are there only for mating.

All ants and termites, honeybees, bumblebees and some wasps live in a eusocial way. In ants there are often different **castes**, for example workers and large soldiers. In Africa, termites build huge mounds that are several metres high. Among mammals, the **naked mole-rat** lives in a eusocial way in underground tunnels in East Africa.

At first sight it is puzzling why animals give up having young of their own. One explanation is that the workers are closely related to the queen and to one another. When they help their brothers and sisters, they therefore pass on many of their own genes. The American scientist **Edward O. Wilson** studied eusociality thoroughly, especially in ants.

Eusocial insects are enormously successful and are found almost everywhere on Earth. Ants loosen the soil, spread seeds and eat pests. Bees and bumblebees pollinate many plants, including fruit trees and vegetables. In Switzerland, beekeepers keep bee colonies that provide honey and pollinate flowers.

begriffe.erklaerung: Each animal takes on a particular task for the community.
A group of animals in a colony with the same task and often the same body shape.
The female that lays the eggs in an insect colony.
All the animals born at about the same time, such as parents and children.

gewusst: In summer, a bee colony can have around 40,000 to 60,000 bees.
An ant queen can live for many years, while workers usually live only for months.

teile.einleitung: Ganesha is one of the best-known and best-loved gods in Hinduism. You recognise him at once by his elephant head. He is regarded as the god of wisdom and as the remover of obstacles.
wichtigste: Ganesha is a god in Hinduism and has an elephant head.
He is regarded as the son of the god Shiva and the goddess Parvati.
Many Hindus pray to Ganesha before they begin something new.
He stands for wisdom, luck and overcoming obstacles.
His mount is a mouse or rat.
Every year the festival of Ganesh Chaturthi is celebrated in his honour.
In Switzerland, too, there are Hindu temples in which Ganesha is worshipped.

abschnitte.text: **Ganesha**, also called Ganapati, is a god in **Hinduism**, one of the great world religions. He has a human body with a belly, four arms and an elephant head. For Hindus, the elephant is a sign of strength, intelligence and a good memory. Ganesha is among the most revered gods in India and around the world.

abschnitte.titel: How did he get the elephant head?
abschnitte.text: There are various stories about his origin. In one well-known story, the goddess **Parvati** shapes a boy and has him guard her door. When her husband **Shiva** comes home and the boy does not let him in, Shiva cuts off his head in anger. To comfort Parvati, he gives the boy the head of an elephant and makes him an important god.

Ganesha is regarded as the lord of beginnings and as the one who clears **obstacles** out of the way. That is why many Hindus pray to him before they begin a journey, an exam, a wedding or a business. He is also the patron of knowledge, writing and art. He often has a broken tusk, with which, according to tradition, he is said to have written down the great epic **Mahabharata**.

Ganesha's mount is a small **mouse** or rat, which shows that even something small can move something great. In his hands he often holds a sweet, an axe, a noose or a lotus flower. His favourite sweets are **modak**, filled dumplings. Figures of Ganesha can be seen in temples, homes, shops and even in cars.

The biggest festival for Ganesha is called **Ganesh Chaturthi** and takes place in August or September, depending on the lunar calendar. In India, especially in Mumbai, huge, colourful figures are built for it and at the end are carried solemnly into rivers or the sea. Many Hindus live in Switzerland, many of them with roots in Sri Lanka. In several Hindu temples, for example in Adliswil or Trimbach, Ganesha is worshipped.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large religion found mainly in India and Nepal.
One of the most important gods in Hinduism and the father of Ganesha.
A very long, ancient Indian heroic epic.
A building in which believers pray and worship their gods.

gewusst: In India, many celebrations and ceremonies begin with a prayer to Ganesha.
Ganesha is also worshipped or depicted in Thailand, Indonesia and Japan.

teile.einleitung: The spring dor beetle is a native beetle that occurs in Europe and also in Switzerland. It often shines a beautiful blue or green and has an important job: it clears away animal droppings and so improves the soil.
wichtigste: The spring dor beetle is a native dung beetle.
It grows to about 12 to 20 millimetres long.
Its armour usually shines metallic blue, green or almost black.
It is on the move mainly in spring and early summer, hence its name.
It likes to live in dry woods and on sandy soils.
It digs tunnels into the ground and supplies its larvae with the droppings of plant-eaters.
Dung beetles help to break down dung and make the soil fertile.

abschnitte.text: The spring dor beetle has a rounded, domed body and grows to about 12 to 20 millimetres long. Its hard armour often shimmers **metallic** blue, green or violet, and sometimes it looks almost black. The wing cases are fairly smooth. On its front legs it has strong teeth with which it can dig like a shovel.

The beetle lives in Europe, including Switzerland, mainly in light, dry woods, on heaths and at sunny woodland edges. It particularly likes **sandy soils**, which are easy for it to dig into. You often see it crawling about on woodland paths. It has its name because it is active mainly in spring and early summer.

Like all dung beetles, the spring dor beetle feeds on the **dung** of other animals, for example the droppings of roe deer, hares, rabbits or grazing animals. It also eats rotting plant matter and fungi. In this way it helps to break down waste in nature. Such animals are called **decomposers**.

For its offspring, the beetle digs vertical tunnels into the ground, which often begin under a pile of droppings. Into these tunnels it carries dung and shapes it into supplies for the **larvae**. The female lays her eggs there, and later the larvae eat their fill. After pupating in the soil, a new beetle emerges.

Dung beetles are important helpers in the **ecosystem** because they remove droppings quickly. In doing so they bring nutrients into the soil and loosen it with their tunnels. Because woods are getting denser and grazing animals are missing, some species of dung beetle have become rarer. On their armour the beetles sometimes carry small **mites**, which in this way get a lift to fresh dung.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another word for the droppings or manure of animals.
The young form of an insect, which still looks quite different from the adult animal.
A living thing that breaks down dead plants, animals or droppings.
Shining like metal.

gewusst: The spring dor beetle is not related to the scarab, which rolls its ball across the ground, but buries its supplies in the soil.
If you turn a dung beetle over, you often see that its underside shines even more beautifully than its back.

teile.einleitung: Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly. At night they hunt insects and find their way, even in complete darkness, using ultrasound and echoes. Around 30 species of bat live in Switzerland, and all of them are protected.
wichtigste: Bats are mammals that fly with wings made of skin.
They find their way using ultrasound calls and their echoes.
The bats of Switzerland eat mainly insects.
In winter they hibernate in caves, cellars or tree hollows.
Females usually have only one young a year.
Around 30 species live in Switzerland, and all are protected.
Bats are important insect eaters and are therefore beneficial animals.

abschnitte.text: **Bats** are mammals: they have fur and suckle their young. Their wings consist of a thin **wing membrane** stretched between the very long fingers, the body and the legs. With their feet they hang upside down from ceilings and branches. The smallest Swiss species such as the common pipistrelle weigh only about five grams, which is as much as a sugar cube. With a wingspan of about 40 centimetres, the greater mouse-eared bat is among the largest species in Switzerland.

As they fly, bats give out very high calls that people cannot hear, called **ultrasound**. These sounds bounce off obstacles and insects and come back as an **echo**. From the echo, the bat can tell where something is, how big it is and how it is moving. This method is called **echolocation**. In this way it catches small mosquitoes in flight even on a pitch-dark night.

All the bat species of Switzerland feed on insects and arachnids. They catch mosquitoes, moths, beetles and flies. A small common pipistrelle can catch hundreds of mosquitoes in one night. Some species pick their prey from leaves or from the ground, the greater mouse-eared bat for example hunts ground beetles. That is why bats are important helpers in gardens, woods and fields.

In summer, the females gather in **maternity roosts**, for example in attics, in tree hollows or behind shutters. There each female usually has a single young one, which she suckles with milk. After a few weeks the young can fly and hunt for themselves. In autumn the bats eat to build up fat reserves. They spend the winter in **hibernation** in caves, tunnels, cellars or tree hollows, where it is cool but frost-free.

In Switzerland, all species of bat are protected by law. Many are threatened because roosts are lost during renovations, old trees are felled and there are fewer insects. Bright street lamps also disturb some species. The **Bat Conservation Foundation** and cantonal offices advise house owners and help when injured animals are found. Anyone who finds a bat should not touch it with bare hands and should call the bat protection emergency hotline.

begriffe.erklaerung: Thin skin between the fingers, body and legs that forms the wing.
Very high sounds that people cannot hear.
Finding the way using sound waves that are thrown back.
A summer roost in which female bats have and raise their young.

gewusst: Despite their name, bats are not related to mice.
In hibernation, the heart of some bats beats only a few times a minute.
Some bats can live to over 30 years old, even though they are so small.

teile.einleitung: The fire salamander is a black tailed amphibian with bright yellow spots that lives in damp deciduous woods. Its vivid colours warn enemies, because its skin contains poison. Especially on warm, rainy nights, you can spot it on woodland paths.
wichtigste: The fire salamander is an amphibian and belongs to the tailed amphibians.
It is black with yellow, sometimes orange, spots or stripes.
Young fire salamanders are born as live larvae that can swim in water.
When seriously threatened, it squirts poison from the glands behind its eyes.
Adult animals breathe through their skin as well as through their lungs.
In winter it rests in frost-free hiding places.
In Switzerland all amphibians are protected, and you must not take them away.

abschnitte.text: The fire salamander usually grows to about 15 to 20 centimetres long. Its glossy black skin has yellow spots or stripes, and the pattern is different on every animal. This **warning colouring** shows enemies that it is poisonous. Behind the eyes are two striking glands, the **parotoid glands**. It usually moves slowly, with a waddling gait, on four short legs.

Fire salamanders live in damp, shady **deciduous and mixed woods** with clear streams. They often avoid open, sunny areas, because their skin would dry out quickly there. During the day they hide under stones, roots or dead wood and come out mainly on damp nights. Many animals stay near the water where they were born all their lives. They spend the winter in **winter rest** in frost-free hiding places, for example in holes in the ground or cracks in rocks.

Adult fire salamanders eat snails, earthworms, spiders, woodlice and insects. They seize their prey with their mouth and swallow it whole. The larvae in the water eat small water insects and the larvae of other animals. A fire salamander can manage for a long time without food.

Unlike frogs, the female does not lay spawn. In spring she deposits live **larvae** in cool, clean streams or springs. You can recognise the larvae by the yellowish spots at the bases of the legs and by the outer **gills**. After a few months they lose the gills and move onto land. Fire salamanders can live to over 20 years old.

In old European legends, the fire salamander was regarded as a creature linked with fire that could survive in it. Probably salamanders crawled out of burning wood in which they had been hiding. In Switzerland it lives mainly in the Jura, on the Central Plateau and in the Pre-Alps, and is on the **Red List**. One danger is an introduced **skin fungus**, which has killed many salamanders in neighbouring countries. Anyone who sees a fire salamander should watch it quietly, without touching it or taking it away.

begriffe.erklaerung: Animals that live in water and on land, for example frogs and salamanders.
Striking colours that show enemies that an animal is poisonous.
Glands behind the eyes that give off a poison.
Breathing organs with which animals take in oxygen in water.

gewusst: The yellow spot pattern is as unique to each fire salamander as a fingerprint.
Its poison can cause skin irritation, so you should wash your hands after contact.
The related Alpine salamander is completely black and gives birth to fully developed young.

teile.einleitung: The quill is the hard, hollow part of a bird's feather, to which the vane is attached. For many centuries people wrote with cut quills, mainly from goose feathers. That is why we still say “fountain pen” and “pen” (the German word “Feder” means “feather”), although pens have long been made of metal or plastic.
wichtigste: The quill is the stem of a bird's feather.
Its lower, hollow part sits in the bird's skin.
Goose feathers were especially often used in the past as writing quills.
In Europe people wrote with quills from about the early Middle Ages until the 19th century.
The tip had to be cut again and again with a small penknife.
In the 19th century, steel nibs replaced the goose quill.

abschnitte.text: A feather consists of the quill and the soft **vane** on both sides. The lower, hollow part of the quill is called the **calamus** and sits in the bird's skin. The upper part, the **shaft**, carries the fine branches of the vane. The quill is made of keratin, the same substance as our hair and fingernails. It is light, flexible and yet very sturdy.

As early as the early Middle Ages, monks in monasteries wrote on parchment with quills. The most popular were large flight feathers of **geese**; for fine lines, raven or swan feathers were sometimes used. The tip was cut at a slant and split in the middle so that the **ink** flowed evenly. To write, you dipped the quill into the inkwell again and again.

Because the tip quickly became blunt, it had to be recut often. For this a small, sharp **penknife** was used. From this the English name for the pocket knife, “penknife”, developed. Good writers could sharpen their quill to a new point in a few seconds.

In the 19th century, **steel nibs** were made in large quantities in England. They were cheap, lasted a long time and no longer had to be cut. Soon afterwards, fountain pens with their own supply of ink appeared. After that, the goose quill was needed almost only by calligraphers and enthusiasts.

Quills are still used today. A professional badminton shuttlecock is made of 16 goose feathers set in a cork head. In old keyboard instruments such as the **harpsichord**, small pieces of quill used to pluck the strings. And in calligraphy courses, people learn how to create beautiful writing with pen and ink.

begriffe.erklaerung: The hollow lowest part of the quill that sits in the skin.
The flat, soft surface of the feather to the left and right of the quill.
The art of writing especially beautifully by hand.
A hard protein from which feathers, hair and nails are made.

gewusst: For right-handers, feathers from the left wing were often used, because they curve to suit the hand.
The expression “from the pen of” still reminds us of writing with quills.
A badminton shuttlecock for competitions contains exactly 16 feathers.

teile.einleitung: The Freiberger is the only horse breed still bred today that originally comes from Switzerland. It comes from the Freiberge (Franches-Montagnes) in the Jura and is known for its calm nature and its versatility.
wichtigste: The Freiberger originally comes from Switzerland.
It has its name from the Freiberge, in French Franches-Montagnes, in the canton of Jura.
It is strong, hardy and has a friendly, calm nature.
Most Freiberger are brown or chestnut.
Freiberger are used for riding, driving and work.
The Swiss National Stud Farm is in Avenches in the canton of Vaud.
Every year in August the Marché-Concours takes place in Saignelégier.

abschnitte.text: The Freiberger is a medium-sized, compact horse with a strong body and powerful legs. It usually measures about 150 to 160 centimetres at the withers. Most common are **bays** with a black mane and **chestnuts** with reddish-brown coats. A friendly look and a good-natured character are typical.

The breed comes from the **Freiberge**, a high plateau in the canton of Jura. The farmers there needed a robust horse for field work, transport and the harsh climate. In the 19th century, the native horses were crossed with other breeds, for example with English and Arabian horses. This is how the Freiberger as we know it today came about.

In the past, the Freiberger was an important **working horse** in agriculture and in the army. In the Swiss army, the horses carried loads through rough terrain. Today it is used mainly for leisure riding, carriage driving and in equestrian sport. Because of its calm character, it is also well suited to children and to **riding therapy**.

At the **National Stud Farm** in Avenches in the canton of Vaud, Freiberger stallions are kept and breeding is supported. Every year in August the **Marché-Concours** takes place in Saignelégier, a large horse festival. There, Freiberger are shown off, and there are races and displays. The festival attracts many thousands of visitors every year.

The Freiberger is regarded as part of Switzerland's cultural heritage and as part of the landscape of the Jura. On the pastures of the Freiberge you often see horses grazing freely among fir trees. These pastures with scattered trees are called **wooded pastures**. To keep the breed healthy, breeders make sure that animals that are too closely related are not mated.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of animals of one species with shared features that has been deliberately bred.
An operation in which horses are bred.
The highest point on a horse's back, where its height is measured.
A horse with a reddish-brown coat and a mane of the same colour or lighter.

gewusst: The Freiberger is the last still living horse breed that is originally Swiss.
At the Marché-Concours in Saignelégier there are also races with farm horses and carriages.

teile.einleitung: The banded demoiselle is a shimmering damselfly that lives on streams and rivers. It has its name because the males carry a dark band on their wings. When it flutters in the sunlight, it looks like a flying jewel.
wichtigste: The banded demoiselle is called Calopteryx splendens in science.
It stands out for its dark banded wings.
The males shine metallic blue, the females greenish.
It belongs to the damselflies.
It lives on slow-flowing streams and rivers.
Its larvae grow up in the water and hunt small animals there.
In Switzerland it is found mainly on the Central Plateau.

abschnitte.text: The banded demoiselle is about 4.5 to 5 centimetres long. The male has a metallic blue-green shining body and in the middle of each wing a broad, dark blue **band**. The female is coloured green-bronze and has transparent, slightly greenish wings. Like all **damselflies**, it folds its wings together over its back at rest. Its flight looks fluttering, almost like that of a butterfly.

The species lives in large parts of Europe and in parts of Asia. It needs **flowing waters** with clean water that does not flow too fast. Sunny banks with reeds, grasses and water plants are important. The males like to sit on leaves that stick out over the water. From there they guard their small territory.

The adult damselflies are hunters. They catch small insects such as mosquitoes and flies in flight. Their large eyes help them to spot prey quickly. The larvae in the water also live as predators and eat mosquito larvae, small crustaceans and other water animals.

The males defend their territory against other males and perform a fluttering **courtship flight** for the females. After mating, the female pricks her eggs into water plants below the surface of the water. Larvae hatch from the eggs and mostly live in the water for about one to two years. Then they climb up a plant stem, the skin splits open and the finished damselfly emerges. The adult animals fly from about May to September.

In Switzerland the banded demoiselle occurs mainly at lower altitudes on the Central Plateau, for example on streams and smaller rivers. It is regarded as a sign of fairly clean water. Where streams are straightened or polluted, it disappears. The **restoration** of streams, that is, turning them back into natural waters, helps it. A close relative is the beautiful demoiselle, whose males have almost entirely dark wings.

begriffe.erklaerung: A delicate dragonfly that folds its wings together at rest.
The young form of an insect, which still looks different from the adult animal.
An area that an animal defends against others of its species.
Making a straightened body of water more natural again.

gewusst: The shimmering blue of the males is not caused by pigment but by light that is scattered by fine structures.
Dragonflies existed over 300 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs.
The larva breathes under water with small gill plates at its rear end.

teile.einleitung: The chamois is a skilful climber of the Alps. It leaps safely over steep rocks and is seen as a symbol of the Alpine world. In Switzerland you can watch it in many mountain areas and also in the Jura.
wichtigste: The chamois feels most at home in steep mountain regions with rocks.
A female is called a doe, a male a buck, and the young a kid.
A doe usually gives birth to a single kid in May or June.
Its horns grow throughout its life and are not shed.
Chamois eat grasses, herbs and lichens, and in winter also buds, moss and bark.
Chamois can jump up to about 2 metres high.
According to the international Red List, the chamois is not endangered.

abschnitte.text: The chamois is about as big as a goat and usually weighs between 25 and 50 kilograms. In summer its coat is reddish brown, in winter almost black and much denser. Typical is the pale face with a dark stripe from the eyes to the muzzle. Both sexes carry hook-shaped **horns**, which are also called **crooks**.

The horns of a chamois differ greatly from the antlers of a deer. They grow throughout its life and are never shed. Every winter a growth ring forms, from which the age can be read. Behind the horns of the buck lies a **scent gland**, which grows larger during the rut and is used for marking.

Chamois live in steep mountain regions with rocks, often at the tree line up to over 2,500 metres high. Their hooves have soft, elastic **pads** with a hard rim, which grip like climbing shoes. The two toes can spread so that the chamois does not slip. This is how it can jump up to about 2 metres high and much further.

Chamois are plant-eaters and **ruminants**. They eat mainly grasses, herbs and lichens. In winter, when little green grows, they also eat buds, moss and bark. Then they often move to lower levels or to windy slopes where the snow is blown away.

The mating season, the **rut**, takes place in November and December. The bucks chase each other across the slopes to win the does for themselves. In May or June a doe usually gives birth to a single **kid**. After just a few hours the young animal can follow its mother over rocks.

In Swiss stories and songs, chamois are often seen as a symbol of the Alpine world. Tens of thousands of chamois live in Switzerland, and on the international Red List the species is not considered endangered. Good places to watch them are the **Swiss National Park** in the Engadine or the Freiberge in the Jura. With binoculars you can often see them standing on rock ledges early in the morning.

begriffe.erklaerung: The female of chamois, ibex and goats.
The young of a chamois, roe deer or goat.
The mating season in deer, chamois and similar animals.
An animal that brings its food back up and chews it again, like cows or chamois.

gewusst: When in danger, chamois give a loud whistle that warns the other animals.
From the long back hairs of the chamois the Gamsbart is tied, a traditional hat decoration.

teile.einleitung: Fire jellyfish are jellyfish whose touch burns strongly on the skin, almost like fire. The term mainly means the hair jellyfish, which are common in the North Sea and the Baltic Sea. Their long tentacles are covered with thousands of tiny stinging cells.
wichtigste: When you touch a fire jellyfish you usually feel a strong burning on your skin.
“Fire jellyfish” is an everyday name, usually for hair jellyfish of the genus Cyanea.
They belong to the cnidarians, like corals and sea anemones.
With stinging cells on their tentacles, they paralyse their prey.
The yellow hair jellyfish can have very long tentacles.
Jellyfish are almost 99 per cent water.
After contact, it helps to rinse the spot with sea water, not with fresh water.

abschnitte.text: “Fire jellyfish” is not a scientific name but an **everyday name** for strongly stinging jellyfish. It usually means the **hair jellyfish**, especially the yellow hair jellyfish and the blue jellyfish. Like all jellyfish, they have a bell-shaped umbrella and long tentacles. They have neither brain nor heart and consist almost entirely of water.

On the **tentacles** sit countless **stinging cells**. In each one is a coiled tube with poison that shoots out in a flash on contact. In this way fire jellyfish paralyse small fish, crustaceans and other jellyfish. In humans the poison causes burning pain, redness and sometimes weals.

Hair jellyfish live in cool seas of the Northern Hemisphere, for example in the **North Sea** and the Baltic Sea. In summer they often drift onto the beaches in large numbers. Most are about 10 to 40 centimetres wide. The Arctic form of the yellow hair jellyfish, the **lion's mane jellyfish**, however, is regarded as one of the largest jellyfish in the world and can have tentacles over 30 metres long.

Jellyfish have a special **alternation of generations**. From the eggs come small larvae, which settle on the sea floor and become polyps. In spring these polyps bud off tiny jellyfish, which swim away and grow up. Most hair jellyfish live as free-swimming jellyfish for only about a year.

You should not touch fire jellyfish, not even when they lie dead on the beach, because their stinging cells keep working for a while. If you have touched one, rinse the spot with **sea water** and do not rub. Fresh water can set off even more stinging cells. Remains of tentacles are removed carefully, for example with a card, and if the symptoms are severe, you go to a doctor. There are no fire jellyfish in Swiss lakes, where only the tiny, harmless freshwater jellyfish lives.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of animals with stinging cells that includes jellyfish, corals and sea anemones.
Long, flexible grasping arms with which animals catch prey.
A tiny cell with a poison tube that shoots out on contact.
A stationary life form of cnidarians from which new jellyfish arise.

gewusst: Even torn-off tentacles can still sting.
The lion's mane jellyfish can be longer than a blue whale.
Jellyfish have existed in the seas for over 500 million years.

teile.einleitung: Fish stocking means that people release young fish into a body of water. The aim is to support fish populations or to build up new ones. In Switzerland, stocking has been usual for over a hundred years, but today it is looked at more closely.
wichtigste: In fishing, stocking means that young fish are released into a body of water.
The young fish mostly come from fish farms.
In Switzerland, mainly trout, whitefish and grayling are stocked.
Stocking is meant to make up for a lack of natural reproduction.
Wrong stocking can spread diseases or push out native species.
Today there is more emphasis on natural habitats than on a lot of stocking.

abschnitte.text: In **fish stocking**, fish eggs, larvae or young fish are put into lakes, rivers or streams. The fish are usually raised in **fish farms**. For this, fish ready to spawn are caught in winter, their eggs are collected and left to hatch in hatcheries. Later the young fish are released at selected places.

Many waters have been greatly changed by power stations, straightening and building work. There, **spawning grounds** and hiding places for young fish are often missing. With stocking, people try to keep the number of fish high for fishing. Sometimes they also want to save rare species or rebuild extinct populations.

In Switzerland, the **cantons** and fishing clubs look after stocking. Brown trout, lake trout, whitefish and grayling are especially often stocked. In the large lakes, fish farms have long helped to support whitefish numbers for professional fishing. Which fish may be released is regulated by the laws of the Confederation and the cantons.

Stocking is not always successful, because many farmed fish survive poorly in the wild. If fish from other waters are released, they can change the **genetic diversity** of native populations. Diseases can also be brought in. Non-native species such as the rainbow trout can push out native fish and may therefore no longer be released in many places.

Today the success of stocking in Switzerland is studied more closely, for example with markings and DNA analysis. Many experts say that good habitats are more important than lots of released fish. That is why rivers and streams are **restored**, that is, made more natural again. Where fish can breed well by themselves, stocking is increasingly given up.

begriffe.erklaerung: A facility in which fish are raised from eggs.
A place where fish lay their eggs.
A body of water is made more natural again, with gravel, bends and hiding places.
The differences in the genes within a species, which make it resilient.

gewusst: From a single female trout, over a thousand eggs can be obtained in a farm.
Farmed fish are often worse at recognising enemies than fish that grew up in the wild.
The rainbow trout originally comes from North America.

teile.einleitung: Flamingos are large, pink waterbirds with long legs, a long neck and a curved beak. They often live in huge colonies on salty lakes and lagoons. They do not have their pink colour from birth, but from their food.
wichtigste: Flamingos form the family Phoenicopteridae and the order Phoenicopteriformes.
Usually six living species of flamingo are distinguished.
The greater flamingo is the largest species, the lesser flamingo the smallest.
The Andean flamingo is regarded as the rarest species.
The pink colour comes from carotenoids in their food.
Flamingos filter their food from the water upside down with their beak.
Their closest relatives are, surprisingly, the grebes.

abschnitte.text: **Flamingos** have very long legs, a long, flexible neck and a beak that is bent downwards. The **greater flamingo** is the largest species and can stand about 1.4 metres tall. The **lesser flamingo** is the smallest species. The plumage is pale pink to bright red, depending on the species, and the wings have black flight feathers. The name comes from the Portuguese or Spanish word “flamengo”, which means flame-coloured, and the genus name Phoenicopterus means crimson-winged.

Usually six species are distinguished: greater flamingo, American flamingo, Chilean flamingo, Andean flamingo, James's flamingo and lesser flamingo. They live in Africa, southern Europe, Asia and Central and South America. The greater flamingo also breeds in Europe, for example in the **Camargue** in southern France and in Spain. The lesser flamingo is the most common species, and as many as around two million animals can gather on the lakes of East Africa. The Andean flamingo lives on salt lakes high in the Andes and is regarded as the rarest species.

Flamingos eat small crustaceans, algae, insect larvae and other tiny living things. To do so, they hold their head upside down in the water and **filter** the food out with fine plates in the beak, rather like a baleen whale. Many of these crustaceans and algae contain **carotenoids**, red and orange pigments. These are stored in the feathers and colour them pink. If flamingos in a zoo are not given food containing pigments, they gradually become pale.

Flamingos live and breed in large **colonies**. They build a cone-shaped mound of mud as a nest and usually lay a single egg on it. Both parents incubate and feed the young one with a red nutritious liquid from the crop, called **crop milk**. The chicks are grey at first and have a straight beak. Later the young birds gather in large groups that are guarded by some adults.

For a long time it was unclear who flamingos are related to. Today the **grebes**, which include the great crested grebe on Swiss lakes, are regarded as their closest relatives. Together they form the group **Mirandornithes**. Several species of flamingo are threatened by water extraction, mining at salt lakes and disturbance at the breeding sites. In Switzerland you see flamingos mainly in zoos, and only very rarely does a single wild bird turn up.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large group of animals that breed together in one place.
Red and orange pigments that are also found in carrots, for example.
An animal that sieves tiny food out of the water.
A nutritious liquid with which flamingo parents feed their chicks.

gewusst: Flamingos often stand on one leg, probably because they lose less heat that way and need hardly any muscle power.
Flamingos eat with their head down, and their beak is then upside down in the water.
Male flamingos also produce crop milk and feed the chicks with it.

teile.einleitung: Trout are fast, spotted fish that live in cold, clear streams, rivers and lakes. In Switzerland they are among the best-known fish and a popular food fish.
wichtigste: Trout belong to the salmon family.
They need cold, clean, oxygen-rich water.
In Switzerland, brown trout, lake trout and rainbow trout are best known.
The flesh of some trout is pink to orange, depending on their food.
Many people in Switzerland go angling for trout because they are tasty food fish.
A popular way of cooking is trout meunière, dusted in flour and fried.
Trout lay their eggs in the gravel of streams.

abschnitte.text: Trout have a slim, streamlined body and small scales. The native **brown trout** can be recognised by red and black spots with a pale edge. The **rainbow trout** originally comes from North America and has a pink shimmering stripe on its side. The lake trout lives in large lakes and can grow much larger than the brown trout.

Trout live in cool, clear waters with plenty of **oxygen**, for example in mountain streams and rivers. If the water gets too warm in summer, they do badly. In Switzerland they occur from the streams of the Central Plateau up to high in the Alps. In a stream, brown trout often defend a fixed spot behind stones.

Trout are predators and hunt insect larvae, freshwater shrimps, worms and small fish. They also snap up insects that fall onto the surface of the water. The flesh of some trout is pink to orange because they eat crustaceans. These contain red pigments called **carotenoids**.

Brown trout mostly spawn in late autumn and winter. The female beats a pit into the gravel with her tail fin, into which she lays the eggs, the so-called **spawn**. The male fertilises the eggs, and then they are covered with gravel. The young fish hatch after a few weeks and at first still live off the yolk sac.

Many people in Switzerland like to angle for trout, because they are a popular and tasty food fish. Anyone who wants to angle needs a permit for it, the so-called **fishing licence**. A popular way of cooking is trout **meunière**, which is dusted in flour and fried in butter. Many trout in the shops come from fish farms, while wild brown trout have become rarer in some waters.

begriffe.erklaerung: The eggs of fish or frogs.
A family of fish that includes salmon, trout, char and whitefish.
A permit that you need for angling in many waters.
Red and orange pigments that are also found in carrots.

gewusst: Lake trout migrate from the lakes up into the rivers to spawn, like salmon.
In “trout au bleu”, the skin turns bluish when cooked, because the layer of slime on the skin is left intact.

teile.einleitung: Fish fins are the body parts with which fish swim, steer and brake. They are made of thin skin supported by fine rays. Each fin has its own job, rather like the parts of a boat.
wichtigste: Fish move through the water with their fins.
The tail fin gives the fish most of its forward thrust.
The dorsal fin and anal fin stop the fish from tipping over.
Pectoral fins and pelvic fins help with steering, braking and holding still.
A distinction is made between paired fins and unpaired fins.
Fin rays support the thin fin membrane.
Trout and salmon have a small adipose fin without rays.

abschnitte.text: **Fins** are flat, movable body parts of fish. They are made of thin skin supported by **fin rays** of bone or cartilage. In perches such as the perch, some rays are sharp and hard, and are called spiny rays. Other rays are soft and flexible. With muscles the fish can raise, fold and turn its fins.

Fish have two groups of fins. The **paired fins** occur on the left and right: the pectoral fins behind the head and the pelvic fins on the belly. In the history of evolution, they correspond to our arms and legs. The **unpaired fins** lie in the middle of the body: the dorsal fin, anal fin and tail fin. Some fish have two dorsal fins, the perch for example.

In most fish the **tail fin** is the engine. The fish moves its rear body and the tail fin strongly back and forth and so pushes the water backwards. This pushes it forwards. In the carp and the trout, most of the thrust comes about this way. Fast open-sea fish such as the tuna have a narrow, sickle-shaped tail fin for high speed.

The dorsal fin and the anal fin work like the keel of a sailing boat and stop the fish from tipping sideways. With the pectoral fins a fish can brake, turn corners or paddle backwards. A goldfish in an aquarium stays in one place with small movements of its pectoral fins. The pelvic fins help with going up and down and with hovering calmly. In this way all the fins work together.

Trout, salmon and grayling have a small **adipose fin** without rays between the dorsal fin and the tail. Flying fish have huge pectoral fins with which they glide over the surface of the water. Seahorses swim mainly with their fluttering dorsal fin. In the ray, the pectoral fins are so broad that they look like wings. In some bred goldfish, the fins are so long that they look almost like veils.

begriffe.erklaerung: A thin rod that supports the fin membrane like the spokes of an umbrella.
Fins that occur on the left and right of the body, that is, pectoral and pelvic fins.
Fins in the middle of the body, that is, dorsal, anal and tail fins.
A small fin without rays in trout and salmon.

gewusst: From the paired fins of ancient fish, the legs of the first land animals developed about 370 million years ago.
Flying fish can glide several dozen metres through the air with their large pectoral fins.
Seahorses beat their small dorsal fin very fast, but they are still among the slowest fish.

teile.einleitung: The Gallic rooster is a well-known symbol of France. You see it on the shirts of sportswomen and sportsmen, on monuments and on old coins. Behind the symbol lies a funny pun from the Latin language.
wichtigste: The Gallic rooster is a well-known national symbol of France.
In Latin, the word “gallus” means both rooster and Gaul.
The Gauls were the Celtic inhabitants of ancient France in Roman times.
The rooster stands for courage, pride and watchfulness.
You can see it, for example, on the shirts of French sports teams.
The official emblem of the French Republic, however, is Marianne.
The rooster is the male of the domestic chicken.

abschnitte.text: The **Gallic rooster** is an emblem of France, much as the edelweiss or the Matterhorn stand for Switzerland. It is not an official state symbol, but it is known throughout the country and around the world. The official emblem of the French Republic is **Marianne**, a female figure. The rooster is used mainly in sport and at celebrations.

About 2,000 years ago, the Romans called the area of present-day France **Gaul** and its inhabitants Gauls. In Latin, “gallus” means both “rooster” and “Gaul”. Even the Romans made fun of this pun. Later the French proudly adopted the rooster as their own sign.

During the **French Revolution** from 1789, the rooster became popular as a sign of the people. It appeared on flags, coins and seals. After the First World War, many French communities put up monuments with a rooster. It stands for courage, pride and **watchfulness**, because the rooster is the first to crow in the morning.

Today you see the Gallic rooster mainly on the **shirts** of French national teams. The French national football team wears it in its badge on the chest.
